Composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara.
The Section on Śrāddha Rites
|| Benediction ||
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

That virtuous soul who daily gratifies human beings with immeasurable *hantakāra* offerings, the assembly of ancestors with faultless and auspicious *kavya* oblations, and the host of gods with abundant *havya* sacrifices;
whose mind is filled with the nectar of bliss flowing from the ocean of meditation on Śrīnātha— [he alone is truly blessed].
This wise Śrī Lakṣmīdhara composes the fourth section, the Śrāddhakāṇḍa.
The Proposition.
The nature of the śrāddha, its divisions, the times and places,
followed by the sacrificial foods, the things to be avoided, and the examination of the brāhmaṇas.
Those who purify the rows [of guests] must be avoided; those unworthy of the row should not be invited.
For one who has been invited, there are specific observances from the time of the invitation until the invocation at the śrāddha.

The excellence of the *śrāddha*, the reception of guests, the sequential rules, the general definitions of the rituals, and the procedure beginning with the silent recitation (*japa*) and the seating.
The ritual resolve (saṅkalpa) for the mantra used in serving the food constitutes the rule for the meal;
here too, the rules for recitation (japa) and so forth apply, as does the sequence of rites following the śrāddha.

The nature of the ancestors and others, the praise of the śrāddha in its proper sequence,
the śrāddha with raw grain (āma-śrāddha), and likewise the śrāddha for one whose father is still living.
Next is the ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha for one who has two fathers; immediately after that, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa śrāddha, and the śrāddha performed subsequent to that.
In this context, even those entitled to perform the *śrāddha* perform a *śrāddha* based on prosperity;
immediately thereafter, the *śrāddha* for one who is still living is described here.
Thus, by the learned Lakṣmīdhara, through the words of various eminent sages,
the section on Śrāddha is explained across thirty-two chapters.

Now follows the ritual for the *śrāddha*.
Regarding this, Hārīta [A. 12] says:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the *śrāddha*. The year is progeny..."

The Lord [is the year]. Its northern course (udagayana), the bright fortnight, and the forenoon belong to the gods. Its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), the dark fortnight, and the afternoon belong to the ancestors.
There is no difference [between them], because [the Lord] is present in his entirety; thus sacrifices are offered in both ways. Because of their intermingling—
Day by day. Moreover, they cite this here:

"He whose two paths carry the offerings to the gods and the ancestral oblations, he whose half [of the world] the ancestors [inhabit], and whose root is the closing of the eyes (time)—the seasons indeed worship him; may he go to immortality."

The two fortnights are the bright (śukla) and the dark (tāmisra). Since time is thus divided for the gods and the ancestors, all time is subsumed within these two modes; therefore, there is "no other state" (nānyabhāvaḥ), meaning no alteration, as it is pervaded by that [time].

"From the Śruti," meaning according to the divisions of forenoon, afternoon, and so forth; "every day, in both ways" means by two methods, namely the divisions of forenoon, afternoon, and so forth; "these two paths" refers to those known as the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna. From this explanatory passage (arthavāda), the Śrāddha [is established] in a general sense.
The injunction regarding what ought to be done is thus postulated.

(1) That specific deity who is heard of as Prajāpati is indeed this very Time consisting of the year. This [Time] has two parts. Of these, the northern course (*udagayana*), the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) constitute one part; "day" (*ahar*) means the daytime. All these constituent parts of the year belong to the gods. The southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) constitute the other part; "night" (*rātri*) means the nighttime. All these constituent parts of the year belong to the Pitṛs. Thus, the year is divided into two halves. Therefore, they say: "The year is Prajāpati. "Of the ancestors" (pitṝṇām) means that the ancestral rite (paitrya-karma) must be performed here. Having reached "that" year, [the month] approaches—that is, comes toward—the person who worships both the gods and the ancestors according to their respective divisions, so that he may become immortal by being oriented toward the fruit of liberation and the like.
Thus is the determination of time according to the division between the divine and the ancestral. (Hemādri, 166–167)
In the *Kṛtyakalpataru*,
the nature of the *śrāddha* has been clearly stated by Āpastamba, as he says:
Āpastamba [2.16.1–4]:
Now, Manu has declared this rite, which bears the name *śrāddha*, to be for the sake of the prosperity of progeny.
In that rite, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities, while the Brāhmaṇas serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. It is performed monthly.
The rite should be performed in the month; the latter half of the month is more auspicious.

Thus, "that which has the word *śrāddha* as its designator" means that which is designated by the term *śrāddha*. "A Brāhmaṇa, for the sake of the *āhavanīya*" means one who is like the *āhavanīya* fire in terms of manifesting the substance.

By virtue of being the locus of the performance [of the rite]. By this, it is stated that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the *śrāddha*—consisting of the relinquishing of wealth for the sake of the ancestors, culminating in the acceptance by the Brahmins—is the primary element.
However, the use of the term *śrāddha* elsewhere, such as in the *deva-śrāddha* and so forth, [is secondary].

The term is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) for the purpose of attaining its specific qualities, just as the word "Agnihotra" is applied to the oblations of the Kauṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice. Furthermore, in this context, each individual—such as the father and so forth—is a deity separately, not the group taken collectively. [This is indicated by] the mantra: "Homage to all the gods. Thus ends the section on the rosary.

"One should offer to those facing east; and for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, by means of their names and *gotras*, to those facing north"— since Viṣṇu [73.13–14] thus specifies each one individually as the object of the dedication.
Then, having taken warm food mixed with sesame seeds and smeared with honey and ghee,
he should [offer it] again using the *devatīrtha* and the *praṇava* alone.
Having said, "This is your food," one should offer sacrifice to all the gods: "O [Name], of the [Gotra] [Name] lineage, this is your food; *svadhā*, obeisance!"

This is also because of the statement in the *Brahma Purāṇa*. As for the plural number in such sentences as "one should give to the ancestors on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyāyāṃ pitṛbhyo dadyāt*), that is used with reference to the act of naming [the individual ancestors], in accordance with their status as distinct deities established by other means of knowledge.
It is like the expression, "Let the Gargas eat. Nor can the father and others, together with their wives, possess the status of a deity; for there is no evidence for such a claim. On the contrary—
In the section on Śrāddha, regarding the nature of the Śrāddha rite:
A woman should not offer [the śrāddha] separately from her husband, except on the day of his death.
For it is traditionally taught that their satisfaction arises solely from the food provided by their own husbands.

Thus, in the statement of Śātātapa, because it is specifically declared that the wife is the cause of satisfaction for the one who receives the funeral cake (piṇḍa) related to her husband, there exists evidence that is indeed the opposite [of your claim].

Thus ends the section on the nature of the *śrāddha* in the *Śrāddhakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara, the son of the illustrious Mahāsāndhivigrahika Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.

Now, the varieties of Śrāddha.

The daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), the rite for prosperity (vṛddhi-śrāddha), the sapindana, the pārvaṇa— and the eighth is known as that performed at a social gathering for the sake of purification.
The ninth is declared to be Karmika, and the tenth is remembered as Daivika;
the eleventh is declared for journeys, and the twelfth is remembered for the purpose of nourishment (Puṣṭi).
This has been explained in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "The śrāddha that is performed day after day is proclaimed as 'nitya' (obligatory).
When one is unable [to perform it with food], it may be done with water, even if devoid of the Vaiśvadeva offering."
The Ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha is called occasional (naimittika);
that too should be performed without [offerings to] the gods, and one should feed an odd number of twice-born brahmins.
That which is performed for the sake of desire, for the accomplishment of a desired object,
according to the Pārvaṇa procedure— that too has been described, O Lord of Birds.
That śrāddha which is performed on an occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi) is called the Vṛddhi-śrāddha.
One should perform the circumambulation entirely in a clockwise direction during the forenoon, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder.
One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
This Sapindikarana rite is to be known by means of the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ";
the remainder should be identical to the Nitya-śrāddha, and the Ekoddista rite applies to women as well.

In the section on Śrāddha, the types of Śrāddha are as follows: that which is performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is declared to be pārvaṇa;
or, that which is performed on a festival day (parvan) is declared to be pārvaṇa.
That śrāddha which is performed in a social assembly is called a *goṣṭhī-śrāddha*;
it is for the sake of the happiness arising from the gathering of many learned men and for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
O Vainateya, that which is performed for the sake of purification by means of feeding Brāhmaṇas is declared by the wise to be "for the purpose of purification" (śuddhyartha).
At the time of the impregnation rite, during the Soma sacrifice, likewise at the parting of the hair ceremony,
and also at the rite for the birth of a male child, the Śrāddha is to be understood as an integral part of the ritual action itself.
The śrāddha performed with reference to the gods is here called daivika;
it should be performed with effort on the seventh lunar day and other such days, using distinguished sacrificial food (haviṣya).

If one who is traveling to another country performs a *śrāddha* with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), it is declared to be for the purpose of a journey; there is no doubt that the same applies at the time of entry as well.
The ancestral rite (śrāddha) performed for the nourishment of the body, as well as that performed for the accumulation of wealth,
should be understood as being for the sake of prosperity, or indeed merely figurative.

"Vṛddhi" refers to occasions such as the birth of a son. However, by the rule "the remainder should be equal to the obligatory [rite]," both the Pārvaṇa and the Ekoddiṣṭa are intended as being equivalent to the obligatory rite. Therefore, the meaning is this: since the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa possesses the nature of both, it is performed with the Pārvaṇa method in its Pārvaṇa aspect.
The portion designated for one (ekoddiṣṭāṃśa) would be equal to, or distinguished from, the ekoddiṣṭa rite performed for the son;

and as for the statement "the ekoddiṣṭa is also for a woman," by the use of the term *ekoddiṣṭa* here, it is actually the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* that is intended, even though it is mentioned incidentally in connection with women.

In the phrase "or performed on a *parvan*," the word *parvan* refers to the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth. "Assembly" (*goṣṭhī*) refers to a group of performers of the *śrāddha*. "For the sake of the happiness of prosperity" means for the sake of that happiness which arises from the abundance of the materials for the *śrāddha*, when many learned men perform the *śrāddha* simultaneously due to some particular occasion.
One.

"The established rule is that it is pārvaṇa," such is the reading in the *Śrāddhacandrikā*.

‘For the sake of the happiness of prosperity’ (saṃpatsukhārtha) — thus [it is said] in Śrāddhacintāmaṇi 6; ‘those which are perfect happinesses’ (samyak sukhā ye) — thus [it is said] in Utpala; ‘the rite is called śrāddha’ — thus in Bhāguri; ‘specifically’ (viśeṣeṇa) — thus in Śrāddhacintāmaṇi.
When the occasion for performing a *kṛṣṇa-kalpataru* (black-leaf rite) has arisen and separate preparations for the cooking have been made, one should perform the *śrāddha* collectively.

Śaṅkhadhara states that the śrāddha performed by bringing together a group [of relatives] is called a *goṣṭhīśrāddha*. This refers to the śrauta and smārta rites, such as those beginning with "at the time of conception (*niṣeka*) and during the *soma* sacrifice," and so forth.

This is an illustration. Regarding the *śrāddha* performed when traveling to another country and upon entering one's home, it should be understood that this applies both to traveling to another country for the purpose of a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) and to entering one's home after having completed a pilgrimage. This is according to the *Brahmapurāṇa*, beginning with the words "whosoever... and so forth.
Because of the statement: "In the case of bodily nourishment," that is, when the administration of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and other such means for the purpose of bodily nourishment is to be performed.
Thus [ends the work] by the illustrious Mahāsāndhivigrahika Bhaṭṭa, son of Śrī Mahāhṛdayadhara.
The sections on the Śrāddha rites in the Śrāddhakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara.

1. Whoever, being well-restrained, cheerful, and well-composed, intends to go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrtha), should first observe a fast at his own home and, bowing with devotion, worship Gaṇeśa.
The wise man, gladdening the gods, the ancestors, and virtuous Brahmins, extends his offerings according to his ability and with great effort;
then, having returned, he should again worship the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins in the same manner.
Thus is the statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa* in the *Śrāddhaprakāśa* (1.333).
N 11.4 11 3 11 || Now, the times for the Śrāddha ceremony.

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya [1.217–218] states: "The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, an occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi), the dark fortnight, the two solstices, the availability of materials, the presence of worthy Brāhmaṇas, the equinoxes, and the sun's passage into a new zodiacal sign."
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and even one's own inclination toward performing a śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the proper times for a śrāddha.

*Vyatīpāta* is a specific *yoga*, the moment when the declinations of the sun and the moon are equal. *Gajacchāyā* is as described in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: it is the *yoga* occurring on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) of the month of *Magha*, known by the name *Kuñjaracchāya*.
It should occur when the moon is situated in Maghā and the sun is positioned in Karkaṭaka. Thus (1).
2.7 The times beginning with the new moon (amāvāsyā), which are constituent parts of the ancestral rite (śrāddha), have been proclaimed by Manu and others.

In this context, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is the fifteenth lunar day (*tithi*) of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). It is of two kinds here: *sinīvālī* and *kuhū*. "Sinīvālī is that [new moon] when the moon is visible; likewise, *kuhū* is that when the moon has vanished. Regarding these, those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnikaiḥ*) should perform the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) on *sinīvālī*, while others should do so on *kuhū*. The "Aṣṭakās" are the eighth days of the dark fortnights during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa. In that regard, the domestic...
Śaunaka states: "The Aṣṭakās are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons" [Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.4.1].

Viṣṇu, however, mentions only three [Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.12.1]. Furthermore, in the Brahma Purāṇa, there are four Aṣṭakās. "Vṛddhi" refers to the group of Vedic rites such as marriage, as well as the birth of a son and so forth. "The two solstices" refers to the transits [of the sun] at Capricorn and Cancer.

‘The attainment of a wealthy Brāhmaṇa’ (*dravyabrāhmaṇasaṃpatti*): that time when there is the attainment or acquisition of a wealthy person, whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, is a time for *śrāddha*. The transits (*saṃkrānti*) of the sun into Capricorn (*makara*), Aries (*meṣa*), and Libra (*tulā*) [are such times]. The purpose of mentioning these separately, like the solstices (*ayana*), is as follows. ‘*Vyatīpāta*’ is a specific astrological conjunction (*yoga*). Regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu says: “Śravaṇā, Aśvinī... [and so forth].

"If the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs on a Sunday at the beginning of the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, or Nādaivata (Śatabhiṣaj), that is called *vyatīpāta*. [In this context,] "Nāgadeva" refers to Āśleṣā; "at the beginning" means in the first quarter (*pāda*), if the Moon is there. And the "Elephant Shadow" (*gajacchāyā*) is described in another Smṛti: "When the Moon is in the asterism of the ancestors (Maghā) and is situated in the hand of the Swan (the constellation Śravaṇā), and the lunar day is the Vaśravaṇī (the twelfth), that is known as the Elephant Shadow."

The *Maghā* [constellation] has the ancestors (*pitṛ*) as its presiding deity; the *Haṃsa* is the Sun (*āditya*); the *Kara* is the *Hasta* constellation; the *Vaiśravaṇīyā* is the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*); and *grahaṇa* refers to an eclipse (*uparāga*). (Aparārka: 1.2)

10. The Ten Powers of a Tathāgata The ten powers of a Tathāgata are as follows: 1. The power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*). 2. The power of knowing the ripening of karma according to its causes (*karma-vipāka-jñāna-bala*). 3. The power of knowing the various inclinations of beings (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*). 4. The power of knowing the diverse elements of beings (*nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala*). 5. The power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings (*indriya-parāpara-jñāna-bala*). 6. The power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatra-gāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*). 7. The power of knowing the meditative concentrations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, along with their defilements and purifications (*dhyāna-vimokṣa-samādhi-samāpatti-saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-jñāna-bala*). 8. The power of knowing the recollection of past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*). 9. The power of knowing death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapatti-jñāna-bala*). 10. The power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala*). These are the ten powers of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses these ten powers, a Tathāgata is called "One Who Has Attained Fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya-prāpta*). He dwells securely, having cast off all fear, and roars the lion's roar in the assemblies. He turns the wheel of Brahmā that has never been turned by any ascetic, brahmin, deity, Māra, or Brahmā in the world. This is the first power. Furthermore, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the ripening of karma for beings according to its causes: "This action leads to a painful ripening; this action leads to a pleasant ripening; this action leads to a ripening that is neither painful nor pleasant. Thus, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the ripening of karma for beings according to its causes. This is the second power. Furthermore, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the various inclinations of beings: "This being has such an inclination; this being has such an inclination. Thus, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the various inclinations of beings. This is the third power. Furthermore, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the diverse elements of beings: "This being has such an element; this being has such an element. Thus, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the diverse elements of beings. This is the fourth power. Furthermore, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the superior and inferior faculties of beings: "This being has dull faculties; this being has sharp faculties. Thus, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the superior and inferior faculties of beings. This is the fifth power. Furthermore, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the paths leading to all destinations: "This path leads to hell; this path leads to the animal realm; this path leads to the realm of hungry ghosts; this path leads to the world of humans; this path leads to the world of gods; this path leads to the state of non-returning; this path leads to the state of once-returning; this path leads to the state of stream-entry; this path leads to the realization of Arhatship; this path leads to Pratyekabuddhahood; this path leads to Perfect Enlightenment. Thus, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the paths leading to all destinations. This is the sixth power. Furthermore, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the meditative concentrations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, along with their defilements and purifications: "This is a meditative concentration; this is a liberation; this is a concentration; this is an attainment; this is its defilement; this is its purification. Thus, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the meditative concentrations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, along with their defilements and purifications. This is the seventh power. Furthermore, a Tathāgata truly knows, as it really is, the recollection of his manifold past lives, including their aspects and details: "In one birth, two births, three births, up to a hundred thousand births, in many eons of dissolution, many eons of evolution, and many eons of both dissolution and evolution, I was there with such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and so on. It is the destroyer of all sins, the bestower of all desired fruits, and the means for attaining liberation. It is the foremost of all duties, the most excellent of all sacrifices, and the supreme among all forms of dharma. It is the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the most meritorious of all meritorious acts, and the greatest of all great deeds. It is the most secret of all secrets, the most profound of all profundities, and the most ancient of all ancient traditions. It is the source of all the Vedas, the essence of all the Purāṇas, and the root of all the Śāstras. It is the pinnacle of all spiritual practices, the crown of all yogas, and the summit of all paths to liberation. It is the ultimate goal of all seekers, the final refuge of all beings, and the very heart of the universe. It is the dispeller of all ignorance, the illuminator of all knowledge, and the purifier of all impurities. It is the giver of all prosperity, the granter of all boons, and the fulfiller of all desires. It is the protector of the distressed, the friend of the virtuous, and the enemy of all evil-doers. It is the sustainer of the world, the creator of the universe, and the witness of all actions. It is the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things, and it exists beyond all time and space. This rite, O sages, is known as the Mahābhārata-yajña, and it should be performed with devotion by those who desire the highest good."

In this context, regarding the materials for the *śrāddha*, where there is a connection with a specific fruit (*phala-viśeṣa*), the engagement [of the agent] is for the sake of that subordinate fruit (*guṇa-phala*). Where no connection with a subordinate quality exists, those [materials] are like obligatory (*nitya*) subsidiaries;
therefore, without them, the constituent parts of the *śrāddha* are simply not accomplished. This applies to that which is prescribed in general as food (*abhyavahāra*).
The sacrificial materials intended for the *śrāddha* must constitute the essential nature of the rite as prepared according to what is available.

Devala:
Those who purify the assembly.

One should avoid those among the Brahmins who are unworthy of the company at sacrificial offerings to the gods and ancestors; having examined the Brahmins in many ways, one should invite those who purify the assembly.
In this regard, Manu [3.173–176] says:
"Learn in full, O best of the twice-born, those foremost of the twice-born by whom a sacrificial feast defiled by one unworthy of the row is purified— those who sanctify the row."
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the sacred expositions,
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisauparṇa hymns, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born in a lineage of those who gave their daughters in marriage according to the Brahma rite, one who knows the Dharmaśāstras, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman.

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand gifts, and one who lives for a hundred years— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly.
The *triṇāciketa* refers to a portion of the *Adhvaryu-veda* and its associated vow; because of the connection with these, the person is also designated as such.

(1) "And one who sings the Jyeṣṭhasāman"—this is the reading of Meghātithi; "one who chants the Vedas and sings the Jyeṣṭhasāman"—thus Nandinī reads. (2) He in whose house there are the five fires—the purifying wind and the three sacrificial fires.
"He who kindles [the fires] every evening and morning—that Brahmin is a sanctifier of the assembly. Thus says Hārīta.

(3) There is a division of the Veda for the Adhvaryus known as the *Triṇāciketa*, beginning with the words "Having drunk water, they went forth without grass" (*pītodakā jagmatūṇāḥ*). Because of his connection with the study of that [text], a person is here called *triṇāciketa*. (Meghātithi)
"Triṇāciketa is a portion of the Yajurveda, and it is contained therein," says Kullūka.

Thus: "The lineage (caraṇa) is remembered as being transmitted through an unbroken succession within a family, like [the transmission of] caste (jāti). "Non-confusion of the womb" (ayonisaṅkara) means not producing offspring with a woman of a different caste, thereby ensuring the purity of the lineage. "Belonging to a Ṛṣi-lineage" (ārṣeyatva) means having a paternal uncle (or elder relative) within one's own *pravara* group. "Dharma" refers to the Dharmaśāstras of Manu and others. The treatise on self-discrimination (*ātma-viveka-śāstra*). Retaining what has been studied without forgetting is "stability" (*sthiti*). The hearing of these six is "learning" (*śruta*). Freedom from causing pain to others through speech and other means is "not afflicting others" (*aparopatāpitā*). Not disclosing the faults of others is "freedom from envy" (*anasūyatā*).

"Stability" and so forth constitute the sixfold sacred learning (*śruta*): devotion to Brahman, devotion to the gods and ancestors, equanimity, gentleness, non-inflicting of suffering upon others, freedom from malice, mildness, and absence of harshness.

Benevolence, pleasant speech, gratitude, providing refuge, and tranquility constitute the thirteenfold ethical conduct (*śīla*). Furthermore, there are forbearance, self-restraint, compassion, generosity, non-violence, honoring the guru, purity, ritual bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, austerity, study of the scriptures, and truthful speech.

Contentment and the observance of vows— this constitutes conduct endowed with sixteen qualities. Those who are of noble birth, learned in the scriptures, possessed of good character, established in their vows, speakers of truth, free from physical defects,

and worthy of the *pāṅkta* (the row of guests at a meal)— specifically those who have studied the Vedas on both sides for twelve generations, who have performed the *triṇāciketa* sacrifice, and who possess the three *madhu* hymns— [are such persons].

One who has begotten a son by a wife of his own caste, one who knows the *Triśīrṣa* hymn, one who chants the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who mutters the *Rudra* hymns, one who is a perpetual celibate (*ūrdhvaretas*), one who approaches his wife only during her season, and one who knows the ultimate reality— these are the purifiers of the assembly. That brahmin in whose house the purifying wind and the three sacred fires are kindled morning and evening is a sanctifier of the assembly.

"A lack of hardness of heart" is *amṛtā*. "Freedom from quarreling" is *apāruṣya* (absence of harshness). "Clarity of mind" is *maitratā* (friendliness). The meaning of the scriptural injunction is that, holding the vessel with the left hand and pouring water with the right hand, one should pour it into the hand of the Brahmin using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) of the right hand. With the verse, "Those fathers of ours who have departed," he should give [the remainder] to the left. "O fathers, grant us heroic sons."

"Thus [is] the food. Here, O ancestors, rejoice according to your respective portions; [this is] the sprinkling of water upon the *darbha* grass with one's own hands. Having performed the scattering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) clockwise with this verse beginning "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ," [one offers] the water-offering (*arghya*), flowers, incense, ointment, betel-nut, and various kinds of edible foods.

He should present a water-vessel combined with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds. When the Brahmins have eaten and attained satisfaction, [he should say]: "May my field not be devoid of grass...
The reading in the printed Viṣṇusmṛti is: "yathābhāgam āmiṣi darbhamūle karāvapātraṃ. According to the Vaijayantī, "karāvaṇa" means "karapāvapaṇam" (the placing of the hands as a vessel).
By the inclusion of the word "ca" (and), [it includes] anointing the eyes and other such acts. (Vaijayantī)
In the section on Śrāddha rites, the post-śrāddha duties, page 207.

Having scattered food on the ground and placed the remnants before them, and having asked, "Are you satisfied? and "Is it sufficient?", he should give water for sipping (ācamana) and so forth to those facing north;
then, giving it to those facing east, and then, with darbha grass in hand, he should sprinkle the site of the śrāddha with the words, "It is consecrated" (saṃprokṣitam).

One should perform everything. Then, facing east, having circumambulated [the deity] while reciting "yan me rāma," and having returned, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability. Having said, "May you be pleased," and being told by them, "We are pleased," [one honors] the gods and the ancestors.
He should recite the *śruti* [mantras]. Having offered the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*) with the names and *gotras*,
saying "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should then, facing eastward with palms joined and mind focused on that, make this request to those facing east.
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
Then, with the words "vāje vāje," he should dismiss the Brahmins after honoring them according to the rules,
following them for a short distance, and saluting them.
The mantra beginning with "yanme rāma" and "yanme rāmaḥ śakuniḥ," and so forth.
Having performed the entire circumambulation around the fire with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya), he should offer pure water with his hand in the aprasavya manner.
(1) "Rāma" means a crow; [this is stated] in Devapāla’s commentary on the Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtra (230): "Rāma is a bird."
(2) (3) "Having honored [them] with sacrificial fees," thus [it is stated in] the printed Viṣṇu-smṛti; 165.
In the *Muhūrta-vilāsa-smṛti*, an additional reading is seen: "They should say, 'So be it':
'May our food be abundant, may we receive guests, may there be those who ask of us, and may we never have to ask anyone.'"

Having accepted these blessings with these two [verses], he should follow [the guest] as far as the boundary and then dismiss him. (Vaijayantī: "On the ground"—this is the reading in printed editions; because of the inclusion of the word "all," other acts such as serving food and so forth are also implied.)
It should be performed with reverence. The reading "udakaṃ śanaiḥ" (water slowly) is [the one accepted by] Medhātithi (on verse 3.204).
Therefore, having made the remains of the sacrificial oblation into funeral cakes (piṇḍas), one should, with a concentrated mind, offer them to the ancestors.
According to the very same rite involving water, he should face away from the birds.
Then, being purified and according to the prescribed rule, he should offer those rice-balls;
he should wipe that hand upon those blades of darbha grass for the sake of the ancestors who partake of the scrapings.
Having sipped water and turned away, the knower of mantras, having sipped water three times slowly,
should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors.
One should slowly pour the remaining water near the piṇḍas;
with a concentrated mind, one should sprinkle those piṇḍas exactly as they were placed.
Having taken very small portions from each of the food balls in successive order,
he should first cause those same seated Brahmins to eat according to the prescribed rule.
Having placed the *tilodaka* along with the *pavitra* into their hands,
he should offer that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May this be for them."

‘Apasavyam’ means counter-clockwise (aprada-kṣiṇam). ‘Āvṛtparikramaḥ’ means by turning around counter-clockwise, specifically with the right side [turned toward the object]. ‘Nirvapet’ means he should deposit; the ellipsis is that [he deposits] upon the kuśa grass spread for the sake of the piṇḍas. ‘Śuci’ means unblemished. ‘Tasmāt’ refers to the sacrificial oblation (havis)—

"From the remainder" means from what remains after the *agnīkaraṇa* oblation. "By this water rite" means by the method of offering water for the washing (*avanejana*). "Having poured" means having given. "According to the rule" means accompanied by the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. "Turning toward the north" means facing the north.

"Having performed the transformation for the sake of becoming [the ancestors]. "Accompanied by mantras" means joined with mantras such as "Homage to you, O ancestors, for the sake of the essence" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ rasāya*). "He should pour out" means he should give. "The remainder" refers to what remains after the first rinsing, following the worship of the Brahmins.
Then Devala said: Having taken up a water-pot filled with water and darbha grass,
and having sat down in front of them, he should announce the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍāvāpa).
(1) When morsels of food are being consumed, the essence of the food (*annarasa*) passes into the hand due to contact with heat; that very thing is called "lepa" (the smear). (Medhātithi) (2)
"By the right hand, by the path of the ancestors," says Govindarāja;
[this concludes] the rites following the Śrāddha in the Śrāddhakāṇḍa.
Then, permitted by them, he went toward the southern direction and prepared a site of sand in a clean, smeared-over place.
The mandala should be large, square, and sloping toward the south;
one should draw three lines through its center using a single blade of darbha grass and then discard that blade.
Then, in that place, he should spread out many auspicious darbha grasses with single roots,
all having their tips pointing southward and their bases moistened with water, laying them down evenly.
Then, rising with palms joined in reverence, he should invoke the ancestors:
"May my ancestors be gracious; may my grandfathers depart."
Reciting this, he should remain silent for a moment without breathing;
having invoked [the deities], he should prepare their seats with darbha grass.
When they are seated in their vessels, one should offer water for rinsing;
there, one should scatter flowers and sesame seeds of various colors.
Then, taking the sacrificial porridge (caru) with his hand holding the pavitra grass-bundle,
he should indeed divide the balls of food, smeared with clarified butter, into four portions using a vessel.
Having anointed them with honey and ghee, he should cause them to be thrown onto a heap of kusha grass in the shade of an elephant,
in the shade of a rhinoceros, or in the presence of a goat's grandson.
One should slowly recite the names of the three [ancestors], preceded by their father's name,
with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), the thumb outside the ring finger, and preceded by the mantra, ending with "svadhā."
"O father, [this is] for you and those who follow you"—with these words and others, one should offer the portion for the father;
likewise for the grandfather, and one should act similarly for the great-grandfather.
(1) Hemādri, 1412;
(4) (5) Hemādri, 1418: ‘stṛṇuyāt’ means he should spread out.
(5) "Having washed, one should scatter [them] there"—this is the reading in Hemādri (1421). (6) "'Vapet' means one should place"—[as stated in] the Hārīta-smṛti (1427).
"One should cause [the mantra] to be sown with the words 'Following you... of the father,'" is the reading of Hemādri (1437).
"He should sow in that manner," so says Hārīta (209).
In the Kṛtyakalpataru [21]
One should cast the remaining [portion] as a common ball into the fourth [ball]. Having thus placed those balls, one should adorn them as before.

Having adorned [the fire] according to the ritual manual, the wise one should offer oblations into the purifying fire with sacrificial offerings and the *kavya* mantra, while pronouncing the sound "svadhā."
Having thus offered oblations into the fire, immediately thereafter,
the twice-born should present a bali-offering of cooked food to those funeral cakes (piṇḍas).

Then, after the offerings have been presented, he should give water for rinsing the mouth from those very same funeral cakes (piṇḍas) using that same bowl for the funeral cakes, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Then, taking a handful of the remnants of the oblation, one should perform the offering of rice balls (piṇḍas) for each of the ancestors' wives in succession, starting from the first.
Then, taking a large portion of the prepared sacrificial oblation,
he should offer it as common to the entire circle of his kinsmen.
One should cause to be given, for each individual ball of rice, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), all kinds of enjoyments,
as well as foods to be chewed, cakes, sugarcane, condiments, and various types of meals.
Then, having taken up the water with sesame seeds in the alms-bowl,
he should walk three times continuously around those funeral cakes, keeping them to his left.
Then, having offered salutations with a restrained mind, he should petition the ancestors for a boon, saying:
"May our lineage increase further, and may we have much to give."
Whether it be on the Ekoddiṣṭa day, in another month, or likewise even after a year, this same procedure shall apply; however, here only a single rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered in worship.
Having thus honored the funeral cakes and offered oblations into the fire according to the rule,
he should approach the place where the Brahmins are seated and honor those Brahmins.
Then, one should feed the twice-born with the food remaining from the *piṇḍas* according to the prescribed rule.

"Of these" refers to the Brāhmaṇas seated for the *śrāddha*. "Beginning with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)" is relative to the performer of the *śrāddha*. "Having come" means having arrived. "Sandy" means consisting of sand.

"Triḥ" means three times. "Tam" refers to that *darbha* grass. "Ekamūlān" means those with many tips attached to a single root. "Udakpādān" means those with roots directed toward the north. "Samam" means at one and the same time.

"Of them" means of the ancestors. "One should prepare their places" implies that these are upon the spread *darbha* grass. "Water for sprinkling" refers to the water for the *avanejana* (ablution). "Bastaḥ" means a goat.
"Apāṅguṣṭham" means with the thumb removed from contact. [The mantra is: "This for you, O father."

The words for the father and others should be used in the vocative case. "Of the remaining [ancestors]," namely the grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth. "As before" means as in the worship of the Brahmins. "With the *kavya* mantra," such as the mantra beginning with "To Agni Kavyavāhana. "Proclaimed" means uttered loudly.

The word "should perform" (*kuryāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Water for sipping" (*ācamanodaka*) refers to the water for the secondary ablution (*pratyavanejana*). Regarding the phrase "and then" (*tataśca*):

the meaning is that one should then envelop the *piṇḍas* three times with a stream of water mixed with sesame seeds while moving counter-clockwise (*apasavya*). And this prescription for the *piṇḍas* by Manu and Devala applies to the Brāhmaṇa—
Although this was already stated prior to the section on food, it is written here in accordance with the context of the section on alms-food (piṇḍa).
Śaṅkha says:
The wise should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) in the vicinity of the leavings;
or alternatively, one should first perform the fire-rite according to the prescribed rule.
Whatever is cooked in the house, whether it be food to be chewed or food to be swallowed,
one must never eat it at the base of the *piṇḍa* without first offering it.
Having fed them according to his devotion, and once they have sipped water and been given sacrificial fees,
he— being of a gracious mind— should cause them to pronounce a blessing, follow them for a short distance, and then dismiss them.
The meaning of "one should not eat without having offered" is that one should offer all the prepared food as *piṇḍa* and *bali*. "At the base of the *piṇḍa*" means in the vicinity of the *piṇḍa*.
Manu and Viṣṇu state that at the first [offering],
one should collect the food fit for all castes, moisten it with water,
and cast it down upon the ground in front of those who have eaten.
(2) The reading "vikiran bhuvi" is found in the Mu. edition.

Having asked, "Was it well-tasted?", he should then cause those who are satisfied to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). Once they have sipped water, he should dismiss them, saying, "May you all be happy."
Immediately thereafter, the Brāhmaṇas should say, "May there be *svadhā*!
For the utterance of *svadhā* is the supreme benediction in all rites for the ancestors.
Then, after they have finished eating, he should offer the remains of the food;
he should act according to what those best of the twice-born say, having received their permission.
At a rite for the ancestors, the word "svaditam" should be used; at a rite in a cow-pen, "suśrutam"; at a rite for prosperity, "saṃpannam"; and at a rite for the gods, "rocana".
Having dismissed those brahmins, self-controlled, silent, and pure,
he should look toward the southern direction and request these boons from the ancestors:
May our donors prosper, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
"Sārvavaṇikam" means everything prepared. "Sannīya" means having mixed together. "Ākāṅkṣan" means looking intently.
Vasiṣṭha [3.69–71]:

One should honor the evening and morning meals with the word "rocate" (it pleases); with "svaditam" (it is well-tasted) for ancestral rites; and with "saṃpannam" (it is complete) for rites of prosperity.
Devala says: When they are thus satisfied, one should give water for drinking as well as water for sipping (ācamana);
one should also remove the remnants of food, but one should avoid pronouncing the names of those belonging to the ancestors (pitṛs).
Then, having taken all the food into the vessel according to the rule,
he himself should pour it out with that vessel into the place where their leavings were set.
And after the twice-born have sipped water,
he should present them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his own ability, consisting of gold, jewels, objects of enjoyment, and other things.

(1) Gobhila and Sāṃkhyāyana state: "The question regarding satisfaction is: 'Was it *svadita*? Medhātithi and Govindarāja, however, explain that even by someone other than the performer, who has arrived at the time of the *śrāddha*, the word "It was *svadita*" must indeed be uttered. Kulaka says: "In the *śrāddha*, this word 'It was *svadita*' must be spoken by someone else; we do not believe this [other view], for it is not supported and increases the confusion."

Then, taking a handful from within the sacrificial oblation himself,
and having grasped both that and a water-filled jar;
Flowing from the tips of the hands of the ancestors and the Brahmins,
he should move counter-clockwise past all of them, facing outward, while offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Having circumambulated it three times, one should cause the water to flow out slowly; then, having carried that vessel around, one should pour it out right there with its mouth turned downward.
Then, indeed, one should have Brāhmaṇas representing the Viśvedevas recite a blessing;
one should have those representing the ancestors recite for inexhaustibility, and finally, [one should offer] water with sesame seeds.
Then, he should salute the Brahmins who have received their portions and are fully satisfied,
first according to the rules for the Vaiśvadeva deities, and then again the ancestors, beginning with the father.
First, he should cause those related to the ancestors to rise while saying, "May there be prosperity";
and once they have risen, he should follow them and collect the remnants from them.
Thereafter, one should likewise cause the Vaiśvarevatya Brahmins to rise;
for these, having previously sat down, are the ones who rise last.

‘Pānīyaṃ’ (water) at the end of the meal [is offered with the mantra]: ‘Thou art the covering of nectar. ‘Evam-patanaṃ’ means that which has such a falling as described above. ‘Caramaṃ’ means afterwards.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One should cause sacrificial grass (*darbha*) with sesame seeds to be placed upon the remains of the food, with their tips pointing toward the south;
and whatever has been offered there to the ancestors,"
Taking a portion from each of those and placing it upon two equal and auspicious vessels,
one should offer the "lid of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhāna*) to the Brahmins, giving it to them one by one.
"O Brahmins, has this been well-prepared for me?"—thus he should say to them;
they reply, "It is well-prepared," and he should address each of them again.
"O sirs, may you be satisfied! they said, "We are indeed satisfied. He spoke to them again, asking, "What remains? And what food still needs to be given?"
They say to him, "Let this be given to the learned (śiṣṭas).
Then, having ascertained that they are satisfied, he should scatter food and water upon the ground.
Those who...
In the Kṛtyakalpataru:

"Those ancestors born in our lineage for whom the rites of offering rice-balls and water have been omitted, those whose tonsure ceremony was not performed, and those who died while still in the womb."
May those for whom no cremation is performed, as well as others who were consumed by fire, be satisfied by what is offered upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.

Then, having washed his hands and likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should remember Hari; thereafter, for the sake of pacifying the expiation, he should relinquish the portion belonging to the deceased.
One should then recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava;
likewise, one should recite the meritorious Madhumatī verses and the words "Madhu, Madhu."

"In the presence of the *ucchiṣṭa*" means in the vicinity of the *ucchiṣṭa*. "For the sake of the pacification achieved through expiation" means for that pacification which is to be accomplished by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Likewise,
an altar should be constructed there in the south-eastern direction;
it should be one cubit in extent from the outer ground and four finger-breadths in height.
Especially for the purpose of offering the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa), this place is most delightful. Oṃ! I destroy all that is impure, as well as all the gods, asuras, and dānavas.
The yakṣas, the rākṣasas, the hosts of piśācas,
and all the yātudhānas have been slain by me.
With this mantra,
one who has well-restrained the self and desires firm and auspicious intelligence should thoroughly mark out the entire sacrificial altar.
And one should scatter kusha grass there with their tips pointing toward the south.
Then, taking a bundle of darbha grass with his left hand,
he should cross over the line in the south with it and recite [the mantra].
Chanting the supreme mantra that wards off demons,
he should spread out the *kuśa* grass roots-downward with their tips pointing south along the line.
In the section on *śrāddha*, regarding the rites subsequent to the *śrāddha*:
Now, indeed, from the cups (*camasa*) and so forth, and likewise from the vessels for the *arghya* offering, [the water is poured].
Taking handfuls of flowers, he placed them individually upon each of their backs.
One should wash [the food] counter-clockwise, while consecrating it with the lineage name and the personal name: "O [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, this food is for you; Svadhā! Homage!"
At the end of the recitation, being well-composed, he should mutter "avanenikṣa";
then, as before, having placed the rice-balls (piṇḍas) in three vessels with water.
Taking warm food mixed with honey, clarified butter, and water, and combined with all kinds of side dishes, one should form it into a ball resembling a bilva fruit in size.
One should offer [the rice-balls] to the grandfather and the others at the base of the *darbha* grass in due order, and should recite: "O [Name], of such-and-such lineage, this rice-ball is for you."
One should recite the mantra "ye ca tvām" separately for each of them;
then, having ritually cleansed both hands upon the darbha grass according to the rules.
Then, having washed [the hands] with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) three times, one should meditate upon Hari;
from those vessels containing the remnants (saṃsrava), the ritual sprinkling (avanejana) is performed with water alone.
Having offered [the water], standing facing north, he should recite "pitaraśca" while contemplating all the ancestors as being satisfied and possessing radiant forms.
While looking [at the ancestors], he should recite with focused mind: "These fathers are rejoicing";
then, having loosened the waist-knot (nīvī), he should mutter: "Obeisance to you, O fathers."
Just as here, having recited that mantra with palms joined in reverence, one should speak separately to each, saying: "O ancestors, this is your garment."
Then one should recite: "O you of such-and-such lineage, this garment is for you," and thus give garments in sequence, including fringes made of white cloth.
When one's age has advanced and one's own hairs have grown old,
one should provide a new thread made of linen, hemp, or even cotton.
One should avoid black wool, and silken garments dyed blue or red; likewise, one should avoid honey, ointments, half-eaten flowers, incense, and unguents.
And one should offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule, so that the piṇḍa may consist of eight limbs.
In the *Kukṣma-kalpataru*, [chapter] 2.
Having worshipped the ancestors who reside in the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), one should bow down, saying:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, the Spring; salutations again and again to the Summer;
and always salutations to the Rains, to the season known as Autumn, and to Winter."
Homage to you, O Hemanta; homage to you, O Śiśira;
and always homage to the months, the years, and the days.

Regarding the phrase "having taken a bunch of darbha grass," the meaning is that having taken a bunch of darbha grass with the left hand, one should scrape [the ground] with both hands. As stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "A twice-born man should perform the scraping with his left and right hands."

"From the statement: 'One should recite the Rakṣona mantra beginning with *apahatā* and so forth. 'Upon their backs,' that is, upon the kuśa grass spread for the sake of the piṇḍas. 'Having given,' meaning having cast [the water].
'As before,' into the arghya vessels for the father and others. 'In due order,' according to the prescribed rule."

With the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), reciting the mantra: "having sprinkled" (saṃmārya) means having sprinkled; "to them" (tebhyaḥ) means to the ancestors present in the rice-balls (piṇḍas); "from those vessels of residual water" (tebhyaḥ saṃsravapātrebhyaḥ) means taking water from the vessels of residual water and giving the water for the washing (āvanejana)—this is the meaning.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa it is said: "Likewise,
the twice-born man should perform the scraping with his left and right hands."
(1) I shall slay all those who are impure, as well as all the gods, asuras, and dānavas, by me.
The Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, along with the hosts of Piśācas, and all the Yātudhānas have been slain by me.
With this mantra, the wise one, with self well-restrained, shall once more scratch the entire sacrificial altar.
Cited in Vīramitrodaya, Śrāddhakāṇḍa, p. 250.
(2) "In the *Brahmapurāṇa*," says Hemādri, 1416–1417;
(3) "One should once scratch the altar with a blade of darbha grass," says Hemādri.
In the section on ancestral rites (Śrāddhakāṇḍa), regarding the ritual following the Śrāddha:
one who desires auspicious intellect should cast [the remains] toward the northern direction, provided he is not a twice-born.
Thus, this has been observed regarding the ancestral rite of that twice-born man;
in this world, the Asuras avoid the śrāddha in whatever place this mantra is recited.
The Rākṣasas indeed avoid that place.
"He should cast"—the ellipsis is "the instrument for scratching."
Likewise,
one should remove the Darbha grass for the sake of the rice-balls all at once, facing the south.
Furthermore, the rule regarding the orientation of the lines toward the east and south will also be explained here.
Devoted to the ancestors, the wise man, having placed his left knee upon the ground, should offer three balls of food mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
One should properly scatter the funeral balls (piṇḍas) while moving counter-clockwise and remaining unwearied,
using various kinds of food, water, flowers, fruits, and edible offerings.
Some men desire that for the maternal grandfathers separately as well,
three rice-balls should be offered in succession, with the thumbs pressed against them and held in a closed fist.
One should diligently offer [the oblation] separately to those accompanied by their followers in due order;
with the left and right hands, one should always recite this mantra.
Saying "Obeisance to you, O Pitṛs; may you be satisfied," he should again, with faith, offer the first piṇḍa with both hands, the left and the right.
"Obeisance to you, O Pitṛs, who are gentle; thus, always remaining unwearied, one should pour water from a vessel onto the line drawn with water."
(1) (2) "He went toward the northern direction," according to Hemādri, 1417.
—Reiterated by Henādri, who adds:

"The phrase 'the northern direction' is used with reference to the *darbha* grasses to be thrown; by this, it is understood that one should throw them toward the southern direction with respect to oneself."
The mantra beginning with "apahṛtā" and others is seen in the *Lekhākaraṇa*.
(1417) 4 (3) According to Hemādri, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, "prāgdakṣiṇā" refers to the direction of safety (*abhayī dik*). 1420.
One should provide a new thread of linen, hemp, or cotton for the Kuṣmakaṃpata tree;
however, one should avoid silk, wool, and silkworm-cloth.
A wise man should avoid [the company of] even those who are unblemished during their period of decline;
for they say that constant application of collyrium is indeed the best remedy for a single eye ailment.
Taking three blades of *darbha* grass, one should perform the rite according to the prescribed rule;
then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should offer excellent collyrium to the ancestors.
And oil from black sesame seeds, well-preserved through its preparation.

"Facing south" (*dakṣiṇāmukhatā*) is an alternative to "facing east, south, or west. "He should circumambulate" (*parikṣipet*) means he should encircle [the site] with the water, flowers, and so forth to be mentioned later. "Counter-clockwise" (*apasavyam*) means not to the right (*apradakṣiṇam*). "And he should avoid the fringe" (*daśāṃ ca varjayet*) refers to [avoiding] anything other than white cloth.

It has ten objects. According to the statement in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, "The venerable one should give garments in sequence, [starting with] the state (*daśā*)," [the first is] the state. "Traikakuda" refers to *sauvīrāñjana*.
In such and such a way,
in that very manner.
Having properly ground the collyrium, the twice-born man should wrap it from the north.
Oil should be offered with the funeral cake (piṇḍa), for it serves as an ointment for the cake;
likewise, collyrium, ointment, garlands, and the offering of thread [should be provided].
One who desires the fruit of the horse sacrifice should perform [the rite] with new, spun silken cloths;
for these ancestors are indeed gods, and these gods are again the ancestors.
This mantra has been proclaimed for these flowers, perfumes, incenses, and so forth;
and at the śrāddha ceremony, one who is composed should recite the Sāvitrī over each individual piṇḍa.
And one should say "to Soma," as well as "to those who have a father."
And here, the Earth should be praised as the sustainer of the funeral offering—
she who belongs to Viṣṇu, she who belongs to Kaśyapa, and likewise she who belongs to Ikṣvāku.
And when fetching water, the Lord Varuṇa is to be praised;
thus says Śātātapa.
In the section on Śrāddha, regarding the rites subsequent to the Śrāddha:
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
One should cause [the practitioner] to recite for the attainment of desired objects and for the fulfillment of cherished desires.
The long rivers and streams, and the three steps of Viṣṇu—
by thus sprinkling water [over these], one shall obtain a long life.
The gods abide in the midst of the waters; everything is established in the waters.
May the waters, placed in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, be auspicious for us.
Lakṣmī dwells in flowers; Lakṣmī dwells in the lotus.
May Lakṣmī always dwell in your cow-pen, and may there always be mental well-being for me.
May my merit be unimpaired; may there be for me peace, nourishment, and fortitude.
May whatever brings about the highest good in this world be granted to me always.

In all cases, however, a great deal should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); may it be so for us. Having accepted their blessings and having circumambulated the Brahmins from left to right, [he should depart].

and having spoken kind words, he should prostrate and bid them farewell.
If the twice-born perform the rite for well-being while the food remains on the plate,

"Once they have sipped water (ācānta), one should offer water, flowers, and beds;

He places those *kuśa* grasses together with their roots into the fire, and likewise that firebrand;

That food which is called "clear" (viśada) by the satiated twice-born is not designated by that name, and it is that which is offered upon the ground.
For those whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, for infants, for those who have just emerged from the womb,

Whatever is given according to this rite near water, upon darbha grass, or upon sand, becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.

"Viśadam" means stainless; the sense is that one should scatter it on the ground after making it fit for scattering. Regarding "by the satiated twice-born," [this refers to] "on the new moon day of the year."

"Near water," and so forth, is the section concerning the results of secondary qualities (*guṇaphala*).
Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 3.247–246; Viṣṇu 81.22–23]:
For women of good family who have died without the sacraments or who have been abandoned, the leavings and that which is scattered upon the *darbha* grass shall be their share.
That which remains on the ground after the meal is declared to be the share for the group of servants at a rite for the ancestors, provided they are straightforward and free from deceit.

(1) "Of those who abandon" refers to teachers and others; or alternatively, "of women of good family" (*kulayoṣitām*) refers to wives of noble lineage whose faults have not been observed, and [the term] "abandoners" (*tyāginām*) refers to those who are independent [in forsaking them]. Others, however, explain that in this context "women of good family" (*kulayoṣitām*) refers to unmarried maidens of noble lineage (*kulayoṣitaḥ*).
(Medhātithi: [This applies to] those for whom the performance of the fire-rite (*agnisaṃskāra*) has been prohibited by such statements as, "The fire-rite should not be performed for him," etc.)

Regarding noble women who have died and departed, leaving their families behind: that portion which is the leavings placed in a vessel and scattered upon *darbha* grass shall be the share of these women of the family; this specific statement constitutes the refined form of alms-food (*saṃskṛta-bhaikṣa*). (Govindarāja) As for the leavings that have fallen upon the ground, that is the allotted share (*bhāgadheya*) of a servant who is not crooked and is diligent. (Govindarāja)

Bṛhaspati [Śrāddha, 110]:

Those among the ancestors who dwell in the realm of the gods are satisfied by what is offered into the fire; those dwelling in the realm of the Pitṛs by the gratification of the twice-born; and those dwelling in hell are satisfied by these three cakes (piṇḍas) offered upon the earth.
Śātātapa and Hārīta state:
"The gods are satisfied by what is offered into the fire, and the ancestors by the twice-born who have been gratified."
The ancestors who dwell among the animals are always satisfied by what is offered upon the ground.
The first ball of rice is remembered as bestowing long life; the second is said to bestow a son; the third indeed bestows prosperity; therefore, one should feed the middle one.
If a wife should desire a son, she may eat the middle *piṇḍa* according to the *prājāpatya* rite; it is traditionally taught that this bestows a son upon her.

"According to the rite of Prajāpati: 'I cause you to consume the essence of the waters and the plants;

Yama says: One should cause one piṇḍa to float in water and present one to the wife.

The moon is pleased by that ball of food which one offers into the waters;
the highly illustrious Moon gratifies both the gods and the ancestors.
And likewise, the wife, restrained in speech and desiring a son, eats the middle ball; thus the great-grandfathers make her possessed of a son.
When the best of the twice-born thus offers another ball of rice into the fire,
he attains eternal worlds and is gratified by his great-grandfathers.

Regarding the phrase "of the eternal ones," [the meaning is]: being "satisfied" (tuṣya), that is, fully gratified, by the great-grandfathers, "he"—the performer of the śrāddha—"attains" (prāpyate), which means he obtains, "the eternal worlds."

"Having extinguished [the fire] in the shade, one should recite [the mantra]. In the case of *ekoddiṣṭas*, that is, in the *śrāddhas* performed on the first day and so forth."
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide for his kinsmen;
having given hospitality to his kinsmen, he should also honor his relatives.
That remnant of food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the dharma is established.
"Consisting mostly of kinsmen" means abounding in kinsmen. Regarding the phrase "then the domestic offering" (*gṛhabali*),
the term *gṛhabali* denotes the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) and is intended as an elliptical designation for the daily great sacrifices, such as the *vaiśvadeva*.
And so it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Having performed the rites for the sake of completion and having sprinkled water around the fire, the knower of mantras should perform the daily Vaiśvadeva sacrifice as well as the bali offering."
In the Āditya Purāṇa it is said: "One should offer the ancestral oblation (pitṛbali) to the ancestors according to the rules and the prescribed rite;
thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering, and afterwards, the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas."
Therefore, the sequence for the Bali and Vaiśvadeva offerings should be understood according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa,
some excellent persons desire the daily rite for the ancestors;
others likewise do not [desire it] for the ancestors, and one should perform the remainder as previously described.

Vasiṣṭha (11.21–22) states:
"In a Śrāddha, the remnants of food must not be removed until the end of the day."
Indeed, those who have not yet performed their water-libations drink those streams of nectar that shine forth.
In the section on Śrāddha, regarding the rites subsequent to the Śrāddha:
one must not wipe away the food remnants until the sun has set.
From there, inexhaustible streams of milk flow for those who participate in the journey.

*Acyotante* means they flow or drip. Regarding the statement "remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) need not be removed," this refers to remnants that have fallen upon the ground. [This is further supported by] the rule: "One should not wipe away a remnant."

This concerns the subject of leftover food-vessels placed on the ground: "Let them share our *sañcara*"; that food which, having been given to one person, is passed on to another is called *sañcara*, and those who partake of it are the slaves and others.

"Then, after the sun has set, having become purified, one should place all the vessels used by the Brahmins into water with their openings turned downwards."
On the second day, the washing of all the vessels likewise brings about infinite satisfaction for the ancestors at all times.
Whatever is cooked in the house— whether it be solid food, soft food, or drink—

his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement.
Therefore, both the giver and the consumer at a śrāddha must be restrained;
if the one who performs the worship is not honored, both shall go to hell.
The term "the bed of a *vṛṣalī*" is an indication for sexual intercourse. Śātātapa says:
"Those who, being overwhelmed, eat at another's *śrāddha* after having already performed a *śrāddha* themselves..."
The ancestors of those who have omitted the rites of offering rice-balls and water fall [to lower realms].
Furthermore, in the Matsya Purāṇa:

"The performer of a Śrāddha and the one who eats at a Śrāddha should avoid all of these: eating a second time, traveling on a journey, gambling, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and [eating] again after having already eaten at a Śrāddha."
One should always avoid private recitation, quarreling, and sleeping during the day;
Viṣṇupurāṇa 2.29.
One who, having been appointed to a *śrāddha*, engages in sexual intercourse— whether as the eater, the one who causes others to eat, or the one who is directed to eat—
causes his ancestors to sink into a pit of semen.
*Vyavāyī* means one who engages in sexual intercourse.
(1) Bṛhaspati: (Śrāddha. 142–144; "The performer of the śrāddha together with those who perform the śrāddha," as read in the Parāśaramādhavīya. (2) Manu, 3.250.
Now, the nature of the father and others.
Regarding this, Manu [3.284] and Devala state:
"They call the Vasus the fathers, and the Rudras the grandfathers."
Likewise, the great-grandfathers and the Ādityas; such is this eternal Śruti.
"The ancestors are to be honored in every way; they are the deities of the deities.
Pure, stainless, and meritorious, they reside in the southern direction."
The Basavas are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas as the great-grandfathers; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.

Whatever rite is performed here by humans on behalf of the *preta*s, the ancestors (*pitṛ*s) are satisfied by it, not the *preta*s; for the ancestors are traditionally known as distinct from the *preta*s.
Yājñavalkya [1.269]:
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha;
[the term] "everywhere" is the reading found in Hemādri’s text. (73)

(2) One should not think that the statement "The *pretas* are not the ancestors" (*na pretāḥ pitaraḥ*)—being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended as a censure—negates the status of the *pretas* as deities (*devatātva*), characterized by their being the intended recipients (*uddeśyatva*) of the oblation; for that would contradict the opening statement, "having intended the *pretas*. Rather, it means: how can human beings who have entered various wombs (*nānāyoni-gata*) possess the capacity to grant specific fruits after having first brought about satisfaction and contentment? [This is what is being denied.]

In order to dispel this doubt, it is stated that the Vasus and others possess the status of *pitṛ* (ancestors), characterized by their presiding over the *preta*s. With this very intention, Yājñavalkya said: (Hemādri, 79) [[page 230-to-230]]
In the section on ancestral rites (śrāddhakāṇḍa), regarding the nature of the ancestors and others:
"Satiated by the śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings."
Paiṭhīnasi (231):
He who, knowing thus, worships the ancestors, [worships] the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
They become pleased with him.
Who indeed are these called "fathers" for whom what is given here becomes inexhaustible?
The Vasus are the fathers, the Rudras are the grandfathers, and the Ādityas are the great-grandfathers; what is given to them here becomes inexhaustible.

In this regard, although the status of the Vasus and others as deities in the *śrāddha* is understood from such statements as, "The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors, the deities of the *śrāddha*," nevertheless, [in the ritual formula] beginning with, "O [Name], of [Gotra] lineage, this is for you,"...
And because of the scriptural injunctions: "This, O [Name], this is for your father," "This, O [Name],
this is for your grandfather," and "This, O [Name], this is for your great-grandfather"—
by means of proclaiming the specific lineage, name, and relationship of one's own progenitor and the others.

Their status as deities is established by their being heard [in the texts] with the dative case ending; they are to be meditated upon in the form of the Vasus and others, according to the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices to the ancestors."

(1) The Vasus consist of those beginning with Agni and ending with the Nakṣatras; the Rudras are the eleven [forms] beginning with Prāṇa; the Ādityas are the twelve months. These eternal entities are the Pitṛs. It should be understood that these alone are the deities of the Śrāddha. Therefore, there is no contradiction. If this is so, what follows for the human Pitṛs? It is said: these are the gods.

The meaning is that Vasu and the others, being pleased, gratify the ancestors of humans—wherever they may be situated—by bestowing the essence of the *śrāddha* offering. Since these [deities] pervade all living beings, their capacity to satisfy the ancestors residing everywhere is not contradictory. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that Agni and all the others have deities dwelling within them as their very core. It was with this very intention that [the author] stated previously as well.

The status of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) as recipients (*saṃpradāna*) has been stated, because it is enjoined that "one should give to the ancestors. Since explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)—which establish the necessity for that [status]—are indeed authoritative, one should not harbor an excessive attachment to the false objections and fallacious arguments put forward by sophists. Now, it might be argued that the Vasus and others are not actually enjoined as deities (*devatās*). To this, it is said: "This very [passage] is the injunction for them."

[Objection: There is a loss of the status of being both ancestors (*pitṛ*) and deities (*devatā*) as previously urged. To this it is replied: there is no contradiction because the Vasus and others are designated as deities (*devatā*), while the ancestors (*pitṛ*) are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*). The term "deities" (*devatā*) is used instead of "gods" (*deva*) for the sake of completing the meter. Since the agent desires to give to the ancestors, the Vasus and others are capable of giving to them wherever they may be, owing to their omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*).
Therefore, this is irreproachable. Furthermore, it should be understood that satisfaction certainly exists for the Vasus and others as well, because they too are spoken of as "givers."

Regarding this, Yama says:

Those who worship the ancestors, the gods, the Brahmins, and the sacrificial fires,

By giving according to this rite, one obtains four boons;
the ancestors bestow wealth, food, progeny, and long life upon the person on earth.
Through the worship of the ancestors, one obtains longevity, sons, fame, heaven, renown, nourishment, strength, prosperity, cattle, happiness, wealth, and grain.
Free from disease, natural, healthy, long-lived, and possessed of sons and grandsons,
one who desires to perform śrāddha shall here become wealthy and an enjoyer of riches.
That man who performs the śrāddha obtains supreme satisfaction in the next world, vast and auspicious realms, and extensive fame.

12]: Whoever performs this meritorious rite of Śrāddha, or even recites it, shall be endowed with all desires and attain immortality.
