Praise of Śrāddha in the Śrāddhakāṇḍa.
The wise person who understands this shall obtain the fruit of faith;
for in this world, both the instructor and the one who gives consent are recorded as having equal merit.
Hārīta [A. 12]:
Neither heroes are born there, nor those free from disease, nor those who live for a hundred years;
nor do they attain any higher good where the Śrāddha is omitted.
Even with roots, fruits, or likewise with offerings of water, one should perform the rite when these are unavailable; one must never entirely abandon the Śrāddha.
In that regard, [it is stated] in the Matsya Purāṇa: || 24 ||
Now follows the *āmaśrāddha* (the śrāddha performed with raw food).
When one who knows the rules performs an Āmaśrāddha,
he should perform the offering into the fire with that [raw food] and offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) with that very same [food].
Jābāli:
For the wise, one who lacks the sacred fires should always perform the *āmaśrāddha*.
Therefore, one should perform the naming rite (*nāmakaraṇa*) with that [uncooked food], and with that same [food] one should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).

The essential meaning here is as follows: "In all cases," when an occasion for a *śrāddha*—such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)—has arisen, one should perform the *anagni-śrāddha*. Here, "without fire" (*anagni*) refers to one who lacks the fire capable of cooking; this, moreover, is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the absence of the entire collection of materials required for cooking. It is not...

Furthermore, [the term] "one without fire" refers to one who has not established the sacred fires; for it is prescribed that those who are uninitiated, those who are without a wife, and those residing abroad may perform the *śrāddha* by means of cooked food.
And likewise in the Matsya Purāṇa: "In that manner,
having taken [the food] with both hands, one should serve it."
With a tranquil mind and darbha grass in hand, he [offered] the water completely.
One should offer auspicious soups, vegetables, and various kinds of foods and edibles,
as well as food with curd and milk, cow’s ghee, and sugar.
O King, when they have finished eating at the conclusion of the meal,
one should consume the food consisting of all varieties of grains, rinsing it with water.
One should cast it away and scatter it upon the ground in front of those who have already eaten;
likewise.
Likewise, in the Śrāddhakāṇḍa, [it says]: "Now, the āmaśrāddha" (235).
Knowing them to be satiated, one should offer water once into the hands of the Brahmins;
likewise, even after they have sipped water (ācamana), one should sip water oneself and offer water once to each.
That remnant, however, should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed.
Having thus described the śrāddha by means of cooking through such statements as these, it is stated in that very chapter:
"Even one who has not been initiated should perform this on all festival days."
The śrāddha known as Sādhāraṇa bestows the fruits of all desires.
"Even one who is separated from his wife, even one living abroad,
even a Śūdra who lacks the sacred mantras— such a wise man may perform this rite according to this procedure.
By this it is meant that the *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with uncooked food) is for one who maintains the sacred fires as well as for one without fires, but only in times of distress (*āpad*).
Indeed, for one who maintains the sacred fires as well as for one who is fireless, the *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha performed with raw food) is always permissible in times of distress;
likewise, a Śūdra may always perform the common *śrāddha* and the *vṛddhiśrāddha*.
"A wise person should perform [the offering] with the mantra *namaskāra*, as if it were raw food (*āmānna*)," because this is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* itself.
Now follows the śrāddha for those whose father is still living, and so forth.
Regarding this, Manu [3.220–222] states:
"But while the father is living, one should offer the oblation to the ancestors alone."
Or else, at a śrāddha ceremony, one may cause even a brahmin to partake as one's own father.
But if one's father has passed away while the grandfather is still living,
he should pronounce his father's name and then proclaim the name of the great-grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu declared;
"or, with his permission, one may perform it oneself at will."
‘Priyamāṇe’ means remaining, that is to say, living. Here, the mention of the name is intended as an indication for the *śrāddha* rite. ‘Śrāddham’.

"For the sake of the *śrāddha*. Regarding the phrase "or, with their permission, at will," this is an alternative view concerning the feeding of the ancestors and so forth. The meaning is that, being permitted by those ancestors and others, one may "perform" what is "desired at will."
Likewise, water is offered to three; the rice-ball proceeds to three;
the fourth is the giver of these; a fifth does not exist.

Viṣṇu [75,1–7]: He who performs a śrāddha while his father is alive should perform it for those for whom his father would have performed it. While both his father and grandfather are alive, he should perform it for those for whom his grandfather would have performed it.
One should not perform [the rite] while the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are still living;
for whomsoever [the term] "living" (*jīvati*) applies—
[Medhātithi].

In the section on *śrāddha*, regarding the *śrāddha* for one whose father is still living (and so forth): if the father has become a deceased ancestor (*preta*), he should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his father, and beyond the grandfather.
One should offer to two ancestors. He whose father and grandfather are deceased should, having offered two pindas to them, offer [the third] to his great-grandfather.
He whose grandfather is deceased should, having placed a pinda for him...
Beyond the great-grandfather, one should give [the offerings] to two [ancestors].
A wise person should likewise perform the Śrāddha for maternal grandfathers;
it should be done according to the rule by substituting the mantras, while for the remaining ancestors it is performed without mantras.

The phrase "the father may have passed away" means that the father alone has died while the grandfather and great-grandfather are still living. Regarding "by means of modification in the mantra," this refers to changing the word "fathers" (*pitaraḥ*) in mantras such as "May the fathers be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*) to "maternal grandfathers" (*mātāmahāḥ*), and so forth.

By the characteristic of the "offering" (prakṣepa). "Of the others," meaning of the paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and so forth. "Devoid of mantras" means that the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) should be performed without mantras.
Hārīta says:
While his father is alive, a son should indeed avoid the time for the Śrāddha;
or rather, it is taught that he should perform it for those same ancestors for whom his father would offer it.
If the grandfather is indeed living, one should complete [the rite] with the father;
and one should diligently offer the water-libation, the lamp, and the collyrium.
(1) "May the fathers be purified; may the grandfathers be purified; may the great-grandfathers be purified" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra, 2.6.14).
(2) When three ancestors, beginning with the father, are living, one should not perform the *śrāddha* at all. One whose father is dead but whose grandfather is living—

And having offered the great *pinda* to the father, one should offer *pindas* to the great-grandfather and the great-great-grandfather. (Vaijayantī) (3) "If [the father] is indeed living" (*sajīve vai*)—this is the reading of Govindānanda (Śrāddhakalpa, 552).
(4) Now, it must be said that the contradiction between these two scriptural statements is to be resolved. True; [this applies] to the birth of a son, the naming ceremony, and so forth.

The statement, "Or one may give even while [the father] is living," pertains to the *nimittaka-vṛddhi-śrāddha* (occasional śrāddha performed on auspicious occasions). The statement, "Without bypassing the living [father]," pertains to other ancestral rites (*pitṛ-kṛtya*). Alternatively, the former statement is intended to prohibit the obligatory entitlement (*nityādhikāra*) in all ancestral rites such as libations (*tarpaṇa*) and the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*. The latter statement, however, is for the purpose of optional performance (*aicchikānuṣṭhāna*) due to the superior benefit (*upakārātiśaya*).

The *śrāddha* that is an auxiliary part of a ritual (*karmāṅgaśrāddha*) must necessarily be performed; otherwise, there would be the consequence of a deficiency in the ritual (*karmavaiguṇya*). (Śrāddhakalpa, 553) [page 237–237] 238
In the *Kṛtyakalpataru* [24]:
"One should not give [the inheritance] by bypassing a living [son]," based on the authority of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*).

One should offer the *śrāddha* with an axe or a hatchet; and because of the statement beginning with "a handful of water," Jayasvāmin maintains that this is an independent rite (*apūrva*), like the *gṛhamedhīya*.
The *Yajñapārśva-pariśiṣṭa* states:
"The Pitṛyajña should conclude with the Homa; for one who knows [the ritual] and whose father is alive, having fed his father, he should offer two other Piṇḍas."
To those ancestors to whom one's father would offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas), the son should also cause them to be offered;
however, he should not offer them on behalf of one who is still living—this is the Vedic injunction.
If the grandfather lives while the father has passed away,
the wise say that the offering should be made to the father alone.
Having placed three morsels [of food] together, he should feed the middle one with it;
he should give two morsels to a Brahmin, or cast them into fire or water.
If both [the father and grandfather] have passed away, yet the great-grandfather is still living,
one should offer two rice-balls for the former [ancestors] and feed the great-grandfather.

One should feed that kinsman who lives among the ancestors, or rather, according to some, one should feed those who are *sapiṇḍas*. It is said that the offering should certainly be given to both those who are living and those who are not.

The *Hiraṇyaketu* [states]: "Because it is a rule of sacrifice and because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the New Moon sacrifice; and because of the scriptural statement, 'He makes this share for these very [deities],' Kātyāyana maintains that the gift is not made even when only one [of the brothers] is living."

Because it is "an injunction for sacrifice" (*yajñavidhi*), neither living nor not living is intended to be expressed. Rather, because it is "an injunction for sacrifice," just as [offerings are made] with reference to one's father and grandfather,
so too a *śrāddha* devoid of Brahmins is performed with reference to the great-grandfather.

Having performed the two *śrāddhas*, one should feed the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) as well with that same *śrāddha* substance, just like the other Brahmins. Alternatively, one may cast the *śrāddha* materials into the fire or into water; however, the *śrāddha* should not be performed directly for the grandfather. This [latter procedure], moreover, belongs specifically to another Vedic school (*śākhā*), as it is not approved by many. (Govindānanda: 555)
The Śrāddha Section: Śrāddha for those whose fathers are living, etc. (239)

This is because sacrifice in the form of renunciation is prescribed as necessary; "because it is a subsidiary part of the Darśa" means that the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is a subsidiary (aṅga) of the Darśa, that is, of the rite known as the Darśa.
Kātyāyana states in the Chandogapariśiṣṭa:
"In the rites involving the offering of pindas for one's father, no entitlement [to perform them] exists."
"One should not give anything by bypassing a living person"—so says the Śruti.
While the grandfather is living, one should perform the offering for the deceased father;
and while that father is aged and living, one should offer for the great-grandfather.
Having proclaimed the name of his father, he should proclaim the name of the great-grandfather—
of the father’s father, and of that father’s father as well.
He for whom the great-grandfather has passed away should offer three funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
A twice-born man may give food and water either to one who is living or to one who is deceased.
"Or he should give to the father's ancestors; he is the father"—this is another Vedic text.
By the phrase "and of that elder," the grandfather is referred to. [The text continues:
"And of him also"—that is, of the father's grandfather, and also of the father's great-grandfather.
'Saṃsthitaḥ' means deceased.

—(2) Gobhilasmṛti, 2, 93–96: "And he who is cherished" (*priyate ca*); "of one who has lived" (*vṛttasya*). Regarding "of one who has lived," this is the reading accepted by Govindānanda (Śrāddhakalpa-kauśalya, 551). "Of the father" (*pituḥ*).
The half-verse, "Having proclaimed his name, he should proclaim the great-grandfather," is not found in the *Gobhilasmṛti* nor in the *Śrāddhakriyākaumudī*.
(1) In rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkṛtya*), such as the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and the *Pārvaṇa*, one who has a living father has no entitlement [to perform them].

He states the reason with the words "not while [the father] is living. In the phrase "of one whose father [is dead]," the word *pitṛ* (father) refers to the father who holds the entitlement (*adhikārin*). Consequently, even while the father is alive—whether he has fallen from his caste, has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), or is incapacitated by incurable disease, old age, or the like—one still possesses the entitlement to perform the ancestral rites (*pitṛkṛtya*). (Govindānanda, 1552)
In the *Kṛtyakalpataru* (The Forest of Ritual Duties) [[page 239–239]].
In the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra* states:
"One gives to the deceased ancestors even if the father is living, and even if the father is hidden by another living person."

For one whose father is living, [the rite] ends with the oblation, or else there is no commencement at all. Jātukarṇya says it does not take place when [the father] is separated [from the son], because of the Vedic text: "One does not pass over one who is living."
For one whose father is living, there are three views:

first, that one should offer to those same ancestors to whom the father would have offered, bypassing the living father; second, that one should perform the rites up to the end of the *homa*—such as "to Soma accompanied by the ancestors" (*somāya pitṛmate*)—in the southern fire; [and third, that one should perform them] in the domestic fire.

Another [teacher] says it is merely a burnt offering (*homamātra*). A third [view] is that "there is no undertaking" (*anārambha*), meaning there is simply no performance of the rite at all. Regarding the phrase "it is not separated," the meaning is that the gift should not be given if someone living is intervening.

In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, which pertains to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, one should offer oblations for those who are living. For those who are all living, the offering is made as a "sarvahuta" (an offering where the entire substance is consumed). If one does not know their names—*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* [2.6.22–24].
To the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.

Regarding the phrase "one should offer to those who are living," one should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to whichever among the ancestors, such as the father and others, is still alive. However, one should give it to the deceased according to the procedure prescribed for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*.
The meaning is that if all [the ancestors] are living, then one should offer three rice-balls.

(2) 4.1.13–27: Regarding that which was stated as the gift for the ancestors, one should give it to the deceased ancestors. He whose father is living is called a *jīvatpitṛka*; he should give to his grandfather and the others, even though they are separated by his living father and so forth. Even a *jīvatpitṛka* should perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. And while performing it...

If any one among the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather is living, one should offer the three rice-balls (piṇḍas) while excluding that living person. This being the position reached, [the author] says: for a sacrificer whose father is living, the ritual known as the Piṇḍapitṛyajña should consist only of the portion ending with the oblation (homa); it should not include the offering of the rice-balls and what follows. Having thus presented this alternative view, he states the established conclusion: "Or rather, there is no undertaking [of the rite at all]."

Thus [it is said]. The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Since the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-dāna*) is the primary element, its performance is not appropriate in its absence; therefore, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* should not be performed by one whose father is still living. He states the reasoning for this: Jātūkarṇya says that when the grandfather and others are separated from the living father and so forth, the offering of the rice-balls does not take place.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Therefore, since the offering of the primary *piṇḍa* is forbidden for one whose father is still living, the position of not undertaking the rite at all is superior. (Vidyādhara’s commentary titled *Saralā*, pp. 134–135).
Now follows the śrāddha for one who has two fathers.
In that regard, the *Śāṅkhāyana-sūtra* states:
"Having placed the rice-balls according to how they were washed—if there is a plurality of ancestors, [they are placed] in a single rice-ball;
there is no [offering] for one whose father is living, nor for one whose ancestors are living. To whomsoever...
Or the father [should perform it] for them, or the son up to the end of the oblation.

"In one [for] both" means both the progenitor (bījin) and the owner of the field (kṣetrin). "In one funeral cake" (piṇḍa) means that he should recite [the lineage] even in a single funeral cake; such is the meaning.
This concludes the section on the Pravaras.

Now, if they have been begotten by a paternal uncle, a kinsman, or one who has the same purpose, they belong to the adoptive father alone. Furthermore, if they have no wife or offspring of their own, they shall take his inheritance and offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to him for three generations.
Although the teacher’s statement that "both [husband and wife] should give" may apply,
one should perform either two *śrāddhas* or one. Or, having designated them separately,
one should mention both the recipient and the progenitor within a single *piṇḍa*, up to the third generation.
It is embraced.
Hārīta says:
"Of these," namely of the seed-sowers beginning with the field-owner and the paternal uncle.

Others maintain that because it is observed that "a field without seed does not bear fruit" and "seed does not sprout in a non-field," the offspring belongs to both; according to them, the progenitor has the first *pravara* (ancestral invocation),
and they should offer two balls of rice (*piṇḍa*) at the funeral rite, or else a single ball.
In the Kṛtyakalpataru [26], two [categories] are mentioned:
in the second, the son; in the third, the grandson and those who share the lepa (the smearings).
Some say that one should announce the names [of the ancestors], including the word *śrī*, up to the seventh generation.

Regarding the phrase "of them": among those ancestors, namely the seed-givers (*bījika*) and the field-owners (*kṣetrin*), one should first designate the most eminent *ṛṣi* of the seed-giver. Then [one designates] the field-owner;
thus there is a state of having two *pravara*s. However, for this [offering], it is performed with the *pravara* consisting of three *ṛṣi*s, in the act of offering (*nirvāpa*).

This is the meaning. "Hutaśeṣa" refers to that which remains after the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation has been performed in the fire.

At the end of the year, one should feed Brāhmaṇas for the sake of the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather. O Pārtha, there is no offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) nor the invocation (āvāhana).

And he should perform [the rite]. He should join the vessel for the deceased (*pretapātra*) to the vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*) with the mantra: "May the earth unite [you], may [the waters] be equal for you. Near the remains of the food, he should fashion four *piṇḍa* offerings. And he should give [remnants] to the Brāhmaṇas who have finished eating...

Having followed them as far as the boundary, he should dismiss them. Then, like the water from the *argha* vessel, he should place the three *piṇḍas* upon the three [spots]. This same procedure applies even when they are in close proximity.
Having thus performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform the *śrāddha* for twelve days, as prescribed for the monthly rites.

Or one may perform it on the thirteenth day; for Śūdras, however, it is on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras. If an intercalary month occurs within the year, then one should increase the duration by one day for the purpose of the monthly rites.

"In the same way, even when the three *karpu*s are present," means that one should join the *piṇḍas* associated with the *ekoddiṣṭa* for the deceased (*preta*) to the *piṇḍas* of the ancestors (*pitṛ*, etc.), even though they are situated near the three *karpu*s.

"Like those performed on the monthly occasion" refers to the *śrāddhas* that occur every month (*māsika*). "Monthly... [The text continues: *māsi...* [is explained as] *māsi bhavāni śrāddhāni*. *Māsi-*... [The term *māsika* is derived from *māsa*].

What is the meaning of that? It refers to the *śrāddhas* for the monthly purposes, which include the propitiation of the *preta* (the deceased) and so forth. Upon the cessation of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), having performed [the rites] during the twelve days, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on this thirteenth day. This is the first [point].
The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Rite in the Section on Śrāddha 255

And the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is performed precisely at the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*). Even the rites for those who died before six months, and so forth, must be performed on the sixth and twelfth days respectively. Thus, according to this view, there are sixteen *śrāddha* offerings. And this applies to both those with the sacred fire (*sāgni*) and those without it (*niragni*) at the time of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), and so on.

It should be understood that this applies when there is a cause for the postponement [of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*]. Furthermore, the fact that prosperity (*vṛddhi*) is a cause for the postponement of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is confirmed by the restatement in the words of Śātātapa: "Whether before a year has passed or even when a full year has elapsed, those deceased who have been made *sapiṇḍa*..."
It is to be known through direct perception.
Paiṭhīnasi says: "At the end of the year there is a dismissal; some say it is after nine months."

Furthermore, this procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* lasting nine months should be understood as applicable when there is the occasion for a *vṛddhiśrāddha* at the beginning of the tenth month or thereafter; the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must not be performed prior to that.
Baijavāpa:
Now, regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. Having omitted the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for one full year, when that year has concluded, he joins together four vessels of water.

In the same way, he offers one portion to the deceased and three to the ancestors. He pours that vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors with the two verses beginning "Those who are common. In this very manner, he distributes the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) as he touches them.
"This deceased one has followed you; O fathers, I give him to you.
May it be auspicious! May the remaining ones be born as long-lived."
May your intentions be as one; may your hearts be united;
may your minds be the same, so that you may prosper together.
"Come together, speak together; let your minds be in harmony, as the gods of old, being in accord, partook of their portion.
[Excluding] those accused of crimes, the outcaste, the killer of an embryo, and an unfaithful woman.
One should not extend [the rule] by analogy.
Hārīta states in the Kūṣmāṇḍa-kalpataru:
"But when [the rite] is completed, one should duly perform the animal-śrāddha."
One should offer four balls of rice; among them, one should offer the first.
Having offered the two portions for the ancestors, the animals, and the Lord,
as well as the oblations of barley, according to the rules of the ritual procedure, one should cast the remaining balls of rice into the water.
From that time forward, the deceased indeed attains the commonality of the ancestors;
he finds the world of the ancestors, and from that point the Śrāddha rite proceeds.
For as many hairs as there are on the animal, for that many thousands of years shall it be inexhaustible for the ancestors, provided one is engaged by the prescribed rite.
For as many thousands of years as there are [in that number], he is honored in the heavenly world;
the performer of the animal sacrifice enjoys all his desires, of this there is no doubt.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Having taken one of the four offering vessels with the left hand,
and [holding] the water with sesame seeds with the right hand alone..."
Recalling the mantra "May the Earth unite you with those who are equal," one should pour a fourth portion of water into the hand of the deceased Brahmin.
Then, one should offer [the water] into that same water separately for the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the others with their respective mantras, and with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ."
Having offered half [of the water] to them according to that same procedure and in accordance with the rules from the vessel,
he himself should perform the remaining half afterwards.
Then, by that same procedure, having offered water for washing at the root of the *darbha* grass to the father, he should devoutly offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) as before.
Having offered the ball of rice (piṇḍa) and meditated upon it as being brilliantly radiant,
one should then divide that piṇḍa into three parts with blades of gold, silver, and darbha grass,
and offer them to the ancestors beginning with the grandfather, and to the deceased.
May the earth, Vāyu, Agni, and Prajāpati unite with you.
One should recite this mantra with devotion, as well as the verse beginning with "samānīva. [End of section] Sapindikarana in the Śrāddhakāṇḍa.
One should honor the deceased for the ancestors with two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ."
Then, having formed those three balls into circular shapes, one should worship them with water-offerings,
flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, and unguents.
But having made the father the primary one, others follow again in their proper order;
for when the father has died, he who has a grandfather still living [should offer].
By him, three rice-balls (piṇḍas) should be offered, beginning with the great-grandfather;
and from those, the paternal rice-ball should be assigned as before.
But if the mother has died while the paternal grandmother still lives,
this same procedure should be performed there as well, beginning with the great-grandmother.

Jābāla says: A son who possesses the *sapiṇḍa* fire and the sacred fires (*agnimān*) should perform the *pitṛyajña*. For by not performing it, he becomes a sinner and is indeed born as a slayer of his father.

The meaning is this: immediately after the period of impurity has ended, when the new moon (darśa) arrives, one must perform the piṇḍapitṛyajña and the śrāddha; then follows the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa preceded by the monthly śrāddhas.
One should act only after having first performed [the preliminary].
Yājñavalkya [1.253–254]:

One should prepare four vessels joined with scented water and sesame seeds for the purpose of the *argha* offering; one should then pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessel of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," he should perform the remainder as previously described;
this Sapindikarana rite for a woman is also performed as an Ekoddista.

The meaning is that for a woman as well, the *ekoddiṣṭa*— namely the rites from the eleventh day onwards— and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed in exactly this same manner. Thus says Vṛddhaśātātapa.
A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a learned disciple,
having performed the sapindikarana rite, should thereafter perform the auspicious ceremony.
Just as the covering of a tree with leaves is necessary for women to perform their duties, so too must it be done.
One should act in this manner for as long as one lives, performing the śrāddha ceremony every year.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
How should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a mother be performed by her sons? It is traditionally taught that her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is to be performed together with her paternal grandmother.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [Gobhila 2.102] states:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a mother is declared to be performed together with the paternal grandmother at the same time as that [of the father],
provided she was an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) and has no son."

The meaning of this is: the son should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his mother together with the paternal grandfather and the others; the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) [should perform it] together with the maternal grandfather and the others.
According to the Āśvalāyana-Śrautasūtra and other texts, the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should designate his mother on the first rice-ball offering,
her father on the second, and her grandfather on the third.
Śātātapa and Vṛddha-Śātātapa state in the second [section]:
"The father should perform [the rite] for an unmarried daughter; but for one who is married, the husband likewise [should do so].
When she has settled [in her husband's home], the offering of water with sesame seeds is performed according to each respective lineage."
As long as the wife remains alive, she partakes in the paternal lineage until the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite;
thereafter, however, she partakes in the husband’s paternal lineage.
When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed, she attains a single form with her husband’s ancestors; therefore, she becomes a sharer of their lineage.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, whatever is offered to the ancestors,
it is a settled rule in the *dharma* texts that the mother is entitled to a share equal to all [the sons].
(1) Dharmasūtra, 2.3.16 [[page 258–258]]
In the section on *śrāddha*, regarding *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* (259):
"when she has passed away" means when she is dead; "water with sesame seeds" refers to the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*).

The mention of "mother" (*mātṛ*) is illustrative; the authors of the *Smṛtimañjarī* and others maintain that the rule regarding "partaking of the father’s lineage" (*pitṛgotrabhājana*) refers specifically to those wedded through censured forms of marriage, such as the *āsura* and others. As for the reason given in the verse "But after [the father's death], [the daughter] belongs to the husband and the father," it is "being of one body" (*ekamūrtitva*), and so forth.

By the phrase "after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*," it is stated that when the substance is manifested specifically for the purpose of the father and others, the mother becomes a "share-taker" (*aṃśaharā*), meaning she partakes in the satisfaction.
Bṛhaspati [Śrāddhakalpa, 85, 29, 26]:
"The mother partakes of the Śrāddha, consisting of *asvadhā*, together with her own husband;
likewise the paternal grandmother and the great-grandmother, each with her own husband."
The sons must offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and water (udaka) for women by means of their husband’s lineage,
as well as for their paternal grandmother and father, each according to his own prescribed rule.
The mantras of marriage take away the paternal lineage;
thereafter, the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and water must be offered to women by means of the husband’s lineage.
This is done with the mantra of the fourth oblation (caturthī-homa), accompanied by the words "skin, flesh, heart, and senses."
A wife is united with her husband; therefore, she belongs to his lineage.
Having performed the Śrāddha on the Aṣṭakā days, preceded by offerings to the gods, with vegetables, meat, and cakes...

Having offered oblations into the fire for each of his own *aṣṭakās* according to the procedure for the *aṣṭakā*, beginning with the deities, he should likewise feed the Brahmins for his mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother as before; having honored them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and followed them as they depart, he should dismiss them. Thereafter, he should perform the six ploughings.
At their base, having first established a fire in the northeast and offered oblations, one should perform the offering of rice-balls at the root of each pit:
three pits for the men and three pits for the women. The three pits for the men [should be filled] with water mixed with food.

[28] One should fill [the vessels]: three *karṣa* each with rice and milk; three *karṣa* each with curd, meat, and milk. Having filled them, one should recite this: "May it become a limb of existence."
And may it be inexhaustible for them.
The meaning is that one should fill [the vessels] with this milk and *karpūra* (camphor). According to another [view], one should fill each with three *karṣa*s of curd, meat, and milk respectively.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [Gobhila 2.103] states: "A woman should not offer separately, except on the day of her husband's death;
for it is traditionally taught that their satisfaction comes solely from the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered to their own husbands."
Likewise,
if the grandfather passes away after the father,
the grandson must perform the sixteen śrāddhas, beginning with the eleventh-day rite.
This should not be performed by the grandson if the grandfather has sons;
having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father, he should perform the monthly rites month after month.
If the ancestors have not been consecrated, one should perform the consecration for the father there along with the grandfather, great-grandfather, and further descendants; so said Kātyāyana.

It is the settled rule that one should perform the funeral consecration (saṃskāra) for one’s father by means of the grandfather— even if the grandfather is most sinful, he purifies him, whether he himself be pure or a doer of evil.

"The two ancestors" refers to the grandfather and great-grandfather; where, for some reason, they are "unconsecrated"—that is, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has not been performed for them—even there, [the offering] is together with those two.
"One should consecrate the father" means that one should perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite for him.
Thus ends the section on Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa in the Śrāddha-kāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara.

Now follows the Śrāddha performed subsequent to the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
Regarding this, Śātātapa states:
"In whatever case the offering of these [ancestors] occurs after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
that *śrāddha* should be understood as being like the *pārvaṇa*, except for occasions of prosperity (*abhyudaya*)."
Whether before a year has passed or when the year is complete,
for those deceased ancestors who have been made *sapiṇḍa*, no separate ritual performance is required.
Therefore, the offering of individual funeral cakes (piṇḍa) is prescribed hereafter for all the deceased who have been joined with mantras.
For those who have performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite have indeed accomplished their purpose;
having crossed over the state of being a *preta*, they have attained the rank of the ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*).
He who offers a separate funeral ball (piṇḍa) to a deceased person for whom the sapindikarana has already been performed violates the rule; he becomes a destroyer of his ancestors.

"In a separate ball" (*pṛthak piṇḍe*): in that *ekoddiṣṭa* rite where the ball is offered separately, without being accompanied by other balls, one "should employ" [the deceased] as the deity; this is the ellipsis.
Jābāla,
however, having performed the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) as well as the monthly śrāddha,
[should perform it] according to his inclination on the anniversary of the death of his mother and father.
One should satisfy a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed with the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, it is held that [the offerings] are common to three [ancestors].
The aurasa (legitimate) and kṣetraja (son born of another's wife) sons should perform the pārvaṇa rite every year;
the other ten types of sons should perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
The two black-bodied ones.
Regarding "pitṛyaśas," this refers here to the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*).

On the day following [the death], it should be performed; likewise every month for a year, and annually thereafter; thus, the first rite is on the eleventh day.
Likewise, in the Matsya Purāṇa, it is stated that from that time forward, on the occasions of the Saṃkrāntis, eclipses, and other such parvans;
One should perform the Śrāddha rite consisting of three rice-balls on the anniversary of death as an Ekoddiṣṭa offering.
He who abandons the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite and performs the *pārvaṇa* instead shall always be a slayer of his father and a destroyer of his mother and brothers.
If a man performs the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha on the anniversary of death, he goes to hell;
furthermore, there will be confusion among the deceased when their rites are conflated.
Wherever it is to be offered after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
it should always be given by one who maintains the sacred fire according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure.

And here, since an equal option between the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāhani*) presents itself, the settled rule is as follows: the legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), if they possess the sacred fires (*sāgni*), should perform only the *pārvaṇa* rite on the anniversary. [As it is said: "The legitimate son and the son born of the wife..."
For there is the statement of Jābāla: "The two sons [should perform it] by means of the Pārvaṇa rite."
Wherever it is to be offered after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
it should always be given according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure as desired.

This is also because of the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "The legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the son begotten on the wife (*kṣetraja*) are without the sacred fires (*niragni*); however, the other sons, whether with or without the sacred fires, should perform only the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for the deceased every year. Thus says the author of the *Mahārṇavaprakāśa*.
Bṛhaspati [on Śrāddha; 150]
In the *Pakalpataru* (1):
"The funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for one who has died must be diligently offered by his sons during the *śrāddha* ceremony."
Together with his kinsmen, relatives, dear disciples, officiating priests, servants, and family chaplains.
[30] And here, it should be understood that with the absence of each preceding member, such as a son and so forth, the qualification for each subsequent member arises.
In the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍas*, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, and the pupils shall carry [the body];
in their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*).

In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa [3.13.31–40]: "O King, the son, the grandson, or the great-grandson, or likewise the lineage of a brother, or even the lineage of a *sapiṇḍa*, becomes eligible to perform the rites."
In the absence of all these, the sapinda lineage of those who share the same water [is entitled to perform the rites],
provided there is a connection by means of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) or by means of water on the mother’s side.
O King, the rites for the deceased must be performed by women from both families,
or they may be performed by those who have entered into a communal association.
Or the king may cause [the rites] to be performed for one whose kin and property have been cut off;
namely, the prior rites, the intermediate rites, and likewise the subsequent rites.
There are three types of rites; hear from me the distinctions among their concluding ceremonies:
those performed until the cremation, those involving the touching of weapons and other items, and those which are the final rites.
These [rites] performed monthly in the first and middle [fortnights] are designated as ekoddiṣṭa;
they continue after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa once the deceased has attained the status of an ancestor (pitṛ).

If a sapinda who has no offspring dies, one who is moved by compassion should first complete the period of impurity for him and then perform the ancestral rites as for a father.
One should perform rites such as the funeral oblations for those in the three stages of life;
however, the ascetic has nothing at all to do, nor does he perform [rites] for others.
The preceptor always performs the offering of funeral cakes for his disciples,
having first performed the ancestral purification rites and whatever else is prescribed for his own caste.
The brother himself made [the offering] for his brother whose wife was not present;
he made it for that brother’s son who had no uterine brother.
On the fourth day, their fathers— whether the daughters have been given away or not yet given away— should perform [the rite] for them with well-concentrated minds.
The daughters' sons perform [the rites] for their maternal grandfathers on the following day, and they too always perform those for their own fathers on the second day.
The father-in-law honored his son-in-law, and those [sons-in-law] were likewise self-restrained;
so too did he honor his friends, their offspring, the Vedic scholars, and his teacher.
And on the following day, having first bathed and performed the water-rites, he should perform the śrāddha for all his nephews and grandsons.
When a Sapiṇḍa relative has died and is childless,
the domestic priest or the minister shall first perform that period of impurity and afterwards perform the funeral rites himself.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, never performs [such rites] for those of other castes, whether out of desire, greed, or even fear; having done so, he would attain the state of that same caste.
Sons born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes perform [funeral rites] for a Brahmin;
he, however, never performs them for such sons.
Their mother performs [services] for them, and they likewise perform [services] for her.
"One who has his own lineage" (*svagotra*) means one for whom a *sagotra* (a kinsman of the same lineage) exists; that is,
when a *sagotra* exists for the person for whom the *śrāddha* is to be performed, [it should not be performed] by someone of a different lineage (*anyagotra*).

A king who is included within a *saṅghāta* (an assembly or corporation) should not perform a *śrāddha*. Even for one whose vows are not yet completed, it is "like a father," meaning just as a father [provides for] his son, in whatever manner and to whatever extent.
In the section on *śrāddha*, regarding those entitled to perform the *śrāddha*:
"Even one who is not of the same *piṇḍa* lineage, if he is endowed with compassion, should perform the rite. [And] for the ascetic (*yati*)...
The statement "nothing at all should be done" refers to the funeral rites for the deceased, beginning with cremation and ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony.
Thus it is said in the Mahābhārata:
Vidura must never be burned, he must never be burned;
for one whose body has already been consumed by knowledge, there is no further burning.
"And that which is prescribed by one's own caste," such as the touching of water, weapons, and so forth at the end of the period of impurity;
[as stated] in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
In the absence of all these, women should perform [the rite] for their mothers without mantras;
in their absence, however, the king should have it performed as if for his own family.
"All rites such as cremation and the rest should be performed correctly by men of the same caste;
in the absence of all [male relatives], women should perform them for their husbands without mantras"—
this refers to women other than the wife, such as concubines (*avaruddhā*) and so forth.
If the brother's wife is not present, the brother himself performed [the rite] for his brother;
this is because the authority of the wife is shown to exist only prior to that point.
Likewise,
for women also, this very same rule has been pointed out and declared;
however, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for them does not exist in the absence of a son.
Every year, men should perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite for a woman on her anniversary of death,
according to the rule that has been declared here for men.

"‘The same applies to women as well’: by whatever relationship— such as that of paternal uncle and so forth— the eleventh-day rite and others are performed for men, by that very same relationship they must also be performed for women."
Now follows the rite for prosperity.
In that regard, the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.13.5–6] states:
"At the marriages of daughters and sons, at the entry into a new house,
and likewise..."
Likewise, in the naming ceremony of children, as well as in the tonsure ceremony and others.
At the parting of the hair ceremony and upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the self-restrained householder should worship the Nāndīmukha class of ancestors.
O lord of men, one should feed an even number of Brahmins facing the east on auspicious occasions such as festivals,
joy, the birth of offspring, marriages, and other such celebrations, according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
The mothers are to be honored first, and the fathers immediately thereafter.
Then likewise the maternal grandfathers and the Viśvedevas;
thus it is stated in the Brahmapurāṇa.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
these, whose faces are bathed in tears, are proclaimed to be the ancestors (pitṛs).
Those who are even earlier than them, who possess offspring and have thrived in happiness, are called the Nāndīmukhas; "nāndī" is said to mean prosperity.
Furthermore, in rites for prosperity that are auspicious and beautiful—
such as at a birth, the initiation ceremony, or the marriage of a son— [one should perform the worship].
(1) Viṣṇupurāṇa, 3.13.20: "One should feed an even number of twice-born [guests] at will day after day"— this is the reading in the Gorakhapur manuscript.
Likewise, in the Śrāddhakāṇḍa [it is said]: "In the case of the *ābhyudayika* rite,
one should satisfy the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed rule."
One should recite the Śakunisūkta as well as the auspicious Svastisūkta.

With devotion and palms joined in reverence, he should invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors while reciting the sacred mantra: "O Viśvedevas, come hither! Then, having spread auspicious Darbha grass upon a verdant meadow, he should likewise orient it facing the east.
One should offer great medicinal herbs as fuel-wood in the fire for the purpose of destroying demons;
likewise, one should scatter there highly praised sesame seeds and barley grains.
One should not perform any rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya);
one should offer food with the divine (daiva) part of the hand while reciting the *svadhā* mantra.
"Is this well-prepared for me?"—thus he should ask them, gladdening them;
and they should say to him, "It is well-prepared," and then he should cast [the oblation] for the attainment of all success.
He should mutter, "May this be inexhaustible for the Nāndīmukhas," and then he should offer darbha grass with milk for the ritual rinsing (avanejana) while facing eastward.
Having given [these offerings] to the Nāndīmukha ancestors, he proceeds toward the eastern direction in due order,
offering rice cooked with śāli grains mixed with curd and honey, as well as jujubes and barley.
Having mixed together the four [substances] into balls resembling bilva fruits,
one should offer them according to the prescribed rite to the ancestors who are nāndīmukha.
One should offer water for the guest-offering (argha), flowers, incense, excellent unguents,
and a pair of new, unwashed garments that are equal and of good quality.
One should then offer grapes, roots of āmalaka, and barley;
likewise, one should always give these to the Brahmins as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having offered milk and barley water in place of the water for inexhaustibility,
[he offers it] to those known as the great-grandfathers and to the mothers with the *nāndīmukha* designation.
Indeed, [offerings are made] to the maternal great-grandmother, paternal great-grandmother, and paternal great-great-grandmother;
and likewise to the maternal grandfathers who are the recipients of the Nāndīmukha rite.
And let the word "svadhā" be uttered by you for those known as the great-grandfathers.
"May there be 'svasti' upon the black-leafed tree," they say to him with laughter, wishing him well.
"May the Viśvedevas be pleased," the donor says to them;
they, being pleased, speak to him in sweet syllables: "May you be pleased."
Reciting "tam ū ṣu vājinam," he should dismiss them;
then follows the excellent Śrāddha for the Nāndīmukhī Mothers.
By this procedure, the work should be performed in rites such as the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair).

"Common" (*sama*) means shared and singular; the meaning is that it is not distinct for each individual *piṇḍa*. "Root" (*mūla*) refers to ginger and the like. "Loud laughter" (*prahasāḥ*) means excessive laughter. And here:

Based on the observation of Kātyāyana’s statement beginning with "The *nāndīmukha* ancestors, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers," it follows that the deities are indeed the father and the others, qualified by the term *nāndīmukha*. As for that which is [stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa* regarding the triad beginning with the father...

Having stated that [the ancestors] are *nāndīmukhas*, the subsequent designation of others as *nāndīmukha* deities of the *vṛddhiśrāddha* is for the purpose of establishing the status of deity in the *vṛddhiśrāddha* even for one whose father and other ancestors are living. Consequently, that [śrāddha] must also necessarily be performed by him.
Regarding this: that *śrāddha* which is performed on the new-moon day (*pārvaṇa*) and so forth should not be performed by him.
For there is a prohibition in the Viṣṇusmṛti stating: "One should not perform [the rite] at all while the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are alive."
Kātyāyana states:

"In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the ritual procedure is performed from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*). In the forenoon, there is the recitation of mantras, excluding those dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*). The *darbha* grasses are straight. Barley (*yava*) serves the purpose of sesame seeds (*tila*). [The word used is] 'it is prepared' (*saṃpannam*')."

The question regarding satiety: [The others should say, "It is well-prepared. The rice-balls (piṇḍas) are mixed with curd, *soma*-juice, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). He asks, "Shall I invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors?
Being authorized with the response, "Invoke them," he says, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased."

At the place for the inexhaustible [offering], he asks, "I shall cause the Nāndīmukha ancestors to be invoked. Being permitted with the words, "Let them be invoked," [he says: "The Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers...
(Śrāddhakalpasūtra, Kātyāyanīya 6.1–12).
The Section on Śrāddha, Chapter 271: The Rite for Prosperity (Ābhyudayika) [pages 268–268]

One should not utter "svadhā," thinking, "May the great-grandfathers—and [the maternal grandfather, the maternal great-grandfather, and the maternal great-great-grandfather]—be pleased. One should feed an even number of guests.
Yājñavalkya [1.250]:
Having thus circumambulated clockwise, one should worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors on the occasion of prosperity;
the offerings should consist of balls of rice mixed with curd and jujube fruits, and the rites should be performed with barley.
Śātātapa says:
A wise person seeking prosperity should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) intended for the gods during the forenoon,
using the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savya), and with straight blades of kuśa grass.
If one offers the Vṛddhi-śrāddha with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) due to a transgression of the proper sequence,
neither the gods nor the ancestors are satisfied according to the prescribed rule.
Assuming the form of the ancestors, the deity partakes of the food;
therefore, in rites for prosperity (vṛddhi-śrāddha), the offering should always be given with the left hand.
On the occasion of a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), one who is self-controlled and pure should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas;
he should cause them to recite: "May the ancestors, whose faces are turned toward the rite, be satisfied."
The Śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed immediately by that for the paternal ancestors;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—thus, at a Vṛddhi ceremony, three Śrāddhas are prescribed.
In all three of these [rites], the pure person should feed an even number of Brahmins;
he should offer [the offerings] with the left hand turned clockwise, beginning with the deities.
The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers, and the Ādityas likewise as the great-grandfathers; such is the scriptural tradition of the Vedas.
One should not perform the *apasavya* rite, nor should one fail to circumambulate clockwise;
for just as one should worship the gods, so too should one worship the ancestors during the *vṛddhi* rites.
With the sacred grass in hand, having sipped water, seated and composed, facing the east, and remaining silent,
he should offer the rice-balls with his left hand during the rite for prosperity (vṛddhi).

252. At rites for prosperity, one should offer the rice-balls upon black, trembling branches, at the tips of Darbha grass, and upon the points of the blades.
Likewise, at the Pārvaṇa rite and the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, the sacrificial grass (dakṣiṇā) should have its tips pointing southward.
One should perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for the fathers, but one should also perform the rite dedicated to the goddesses;
even before those, the Mothers must be worshipped with great effort.
If one serves food at a śrāddha ceremony without having performed the Mātṛ-yāga,
the Mothers, possessed by wrath, will seek to cause him harm.

"Daivikam" here refers to the *abhyudayika* (prosperity) rite, because the Nāndīmukha ancestors are treated like gods. "He should cause [them] to say, 'May they be satisfied,'" with the understanding that this is at the place where the *akṣayya* (imperishable) water is offered. "Mātṛyāgaḥ" means the worship of the mothers.

In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, in the section concerning prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), it is stated: "Some men desire [the rite] even when the *vaiśvadeva* is omitted. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, verses 1.13–19: 13. One should perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice every day with cooked food; for that is declared to be the highest duty for householders. 14. By means of that, one attains heaven, long life, fame, and strength; therefore, one should always perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. 15. Without the *vaiśvadeva*, no offering should be made by a householder; for that which is given without the *vaiśvadeva* does not reach the gods. 16. The ancestors do not eat the food of one who performs the *śrāddha* without first performing the *vaiśvadeva*; they depart from there, having been disregarded. 17. The gods do not accept the offerings of one who performs the *śrāddha* without first performing the *vaiśvadeva*; they turn away from him like deer from a hunter. 18. Whatever is given without the *vaiśvadeva*, whatever is offered without the *vaiśvadeva*, and whatever is eaten without the *vaiśvadeva*—all that goes to the demons. 19. Therefore, one should always perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice with all effort; for without the *vaiśvadeva*, neither gods nor ancestors are satisfied.
In all rites, beginning with those for the ancestors, the Mothers together with their lords of the hosts must be worshipped with diligence; when they are worshipped, they in turn bestow worship.
And upon pure images, those painted on cloth and other materials,
as well as even upon heaps of unbroken rice, with various kinds of food offerings.
One should cause a stream of wealth (vasordhārā) to flow from the corner [of the vessel], consisting of seven streams of ghee, or five streams;
it should be neither too low nor too high.
Having recited there with a concentrated mind those mantras that bestow long life for the sake of peace,
he should thereafter commence the offering of the śrāddha to the six ancestors.
The entire procedure taught by Vasiṣṭha should be understood here as being free from worldly motives;
beyond this, I shall explain whatever specific details there may be in this context.
Having seated the invited Brahmins in pairs on both sides,
he should likewise offer straight *kuśa* grass with his hand.

‘Āyuṣyāṇi’ refers to the hymns that cause the increase of longevity. ‘To six’ means to the three ancestors beginning with the father, and to the three ancestors beginning with the maternal grandfather. And [the phrase] ‘to six’...
[as on page 270].
In the section on *śrāddha*, regarding the *ābhyudayika* rite (273):
this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [the offerings] to the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. "Having invited [them] in the morning..."
By the use of the plural "those," even the optional [alternative] is excluded. "On both sides" means on the paternal side and on the side of the Vaiśvadevas.
Likewise, [Gobhila 1.24–27]:
the invitation for the evening meal.
No one at all should ever place his left knee on the ground;
one should always serve the ancestors here with devotion, just as one would the gods.

Having seated them upon kusha grass after they have been offered [the water] with the words "To the ancestors," one should cause the arghya to be given to the ancestors, addressing them by their lineage names.
In this rite, the practice of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) is not required, nor is the ancestral (pitrya) portion of the hand prescribed;
indeed, the filling of the vessels and other such acts should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (daiva).

Having placed the hands in pairs with the right hand uppermost and the tips of the fingers joined by the *pavitra* grass, the offering should be presented; here, it is not given to each individual separately.

"Jyeṣṭhottarakarān" means such that the hand is placed over the hand of the eldest (jyeṣṭha), who was seated first. "Karāgrāgrapavitrān" refers to those whose pavitra-grass tips are positioned at the very tips of their hands.
Likewise, according to Gobhila (1.39–55),
that threefold silent recitation of "madhu, madhu" intended for those desiring to eat, which follows the Gāyatrī, is here performed without the mantras containing the word "madhu."
While they are eating, one should never recite the *Pitṛsaṃhitā*;
instead, another auspicious recitation, such as the *Soma-sāman* and others, should be performed.
Whatever portion of food there is there, like sesame or barley,
that which remains near the leavings is here [considered] the opposite when the [guests] are satiated.
"Is it well-prepared?"—with this [question], they are satisfied; this is prescribed as the point for inquiry.
When "It is very well-prepared" is said in reply, one should offer the remaining food.
And on darbha grass with tips pointing eastward, having addressed Āya as before;
One should pour water without sesame seeds at the root of a small *kalpavṛkṣa* tree, saying: "May [the ancestors] descend."
The second and third [seats] are for the regions of Madhyadeśa and Apradeśa;
and to their left are those beginning with the maternal grandfather.
Having set aside a portion of all the food, sprinkled it with condiments,
and mixed it with unbroken grains and jujube fruits, he should then face the east.
Having made the rice-balls (piṇḍas) according to the measure of a thumb, like the water-offering (avanejana),
one should then perform the water-offering once more with the water used for washing that vessel.
Even when the balls of rice (piṇḍas) are offered in successive order, each subsequent one should be inferior to the preceding ones in the śrāddha rites for those who are progressively lower.
Therefore, in all śrāddha rites— whether those performed on auspicious occasions or otherwise—
one should offer [the food] slightly adhering to the root, middle, and tip regions [of the kusa grass].
One should silently cast the perfumes and other offerings, and thereafter invite the twice-born.
This same procedure, excluding the *yaṣa* [mantra], should apply elsewhere as well.
[This is done] in a place sloping toward the south, while [the performer] faces the south.
On darbha grass with the tips pointing south—this is the rule prescribed for other occasions as well.
Then, having sat upon the foremost ground, he should say, "May it be well-sprinkled," and likewise,
"May the waters be auspicious," while sprinkling water upon the even-numbered guests.
After this, one should offer flowers with the thought, "May there be joy," and one should present unbroken grains (akṣata) with the thought, "May there be well-being and freedom from misfortune."
The offering of inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) is taught to be like the offering of the half-portion;
one should always perform it on the sixth lunar day, and never on the fourth.
When all [the women] have been addressed with their requests by the best of the twice-born,
he who has placed the vessels face upwards should sprinkle water over the rice-balls (piṇḍas) covered by the sacred grass (pavitra).
Having caused an even number of Brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings, and having always grasped the thumb of the leading Brahmin, one should then bow down and follow him as he departs.

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of the *tilavadya*": whatever procedure involving sesame (*tila*) is performed elsewhere, it should be performed here in such a way that it becomes associated with barley (*yava*).
In the section on *śrāddha*, regarding the *ābhyudayika* rite:
"not inverted" means by way of giving with the deity-tirtha (*devatīrtha*) and so forth; "the first person" refers to the primary male ancestor.
‘Īṣatsaktān’ means slightly attached.
Likewise, [Gobhila 1.58–68]:
"Those rites which are to be performed repeatedly by those who perform rituals,
such as the Mātṛ-śrāddha and the Śrāddha itself, need not be repeated at every performance."
At the establishment of the sacred fires, at the two daily oblations, and likewise at the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice;
at the ritual offering of bali, and similarly at the new moon and full moon sacrifices.
Regarding both the *navayajña* and the ordinary sacrifice, the wise declare thus:
there should be only one *śrāddha* among these, not separate ones for each.

A śrāddha should not be performed on the Aṣṭakā days, nor is a śrāddha desired within another śrāddha; nor [should it be performed] during the rites for a woman about to give birth, the birth-rite, or the rites for one who has returned from a journey.
Regarding the group of rites beginning with marriage that was mentioned,
and the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) which we have heard was at the end— here, one should perform only one [of these] at the beginning, starting with marriage.
The śrāddha should not be performed at the beginning of each individual ritual act.
There should be one *śrāddha* at dusk for the exiting and entering of the cows;
however, it is not appropriate to perform a *śrāddha* during the first rite for prosperity (*puṣṭikarman*).
One should perform [the rites] separately for each of the six, beginning with *halādi* and *yogādi*;
for others, one should perform them all together at the very beginning of each individual application.
For those two who serve food for the sake of the welfare of large cattle and small animals,
and whose rites are dedicated to the Sun and the Moon, no Śrāddha is prescribed.
The *Daśagranthika* alone is not sufficient for treating the effects of a venomous bite;
it is not found to be effective in the treatment of worm-bites, nor indeed in the remaining cases.

When the rites for the Mothers are performed collectively, the worship of the Mothers should always be done only once; the Śrāddha should likewise be performed only at the beginning, not separately for each individual rite.
Wherever there may be a śrāddha, there the Mothers [are present].
And repeatedly on the wish-fulfilling tree.

He states the restriction regarding specific objects for this very [rule] concerning the "eleven rites" with the words, "In the *ādhāna* and the two *homas*, etc."; by that, [the rule applies to] the *soma*-...
In the case of the *pāgāvau*, there is repetition at each performance. "The *āmrayaṇa*" refers to the offering of mangoes.

"Rites for one who has returned from travel" (*proṣitāgatakarmasu*) refers to what is prescribed [in the texts], such as: "Having returned from being away, he stands near the house; having seen his son, he mutters [the mantra]," and so forth. "The group of rites" (*karmagaṇaḥ*) refers to the entry into the house, the fourth [rite], and so on.
"Karmādiḥ" [means] "the mothers"; the word "are to be worshipped" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Likewise,

a father should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) to his own ancestors during the sacramental rites of his sons, up until their marriage; but in his absence, [the son] should do so according to that same order.
"Until the wedding" means up to the point of marriage. Yama says:
"Even for the ancestors, guests are deities at the times of śrāddha offerings."
And the ancestors are always the guests of the deities.

Thus ends the section on *ābhyudayika* (prosperity rites) in the *Śrāddhakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war and son of the illustrious Mahāsandhivigrahika Hṛdayadhara.
Now follows the procedure for the *jīvacchrāddha* (the śrāddha performed while the person is still alive).
In that regard, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"When life— which arises from place, time, wealth, faith, and perseverance— still exists, a man himself should offer the *śrāddha* for the sake of the living."
Having observed the fast and bathed well on the thirteenth day, being composed in mind,
one should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, who is both the agent and the enjoyer.

He is omnipresent in water, on land, in the sky, in images, in the ritual jar, in the lotus, and in the sun; he dwells in the moon, fire, the preceptor, cows, Brahmins, and in one’s mother and father.
With a concentrated mind, he should offer three water-cows (jaladhenu) accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) and sesame seeds to the ancestors in front of them.
Recalling [the mantra]: "Svadhā! Adoration to Soma accompanied by the ancestors! and recalling: "Svadhā! Adoration to Agni, the bearer of offerings to the ancestors (Kavyavāhana)!"
One should place the third [offering] on the right, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), while recollecting:
"Oṃ Māyā Aṅgirase Svadhā Namaḥ."
Having placed the Brahmins between those two, one should seat them upon leaves;
and having first worshipped the Viśvedevas on the day prior to the invitation.
"O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Vasus; I feed you for the sake of the Rudras;
O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Sūryas"—thus he should say to them.
He should perform the remaining rites, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), as in the ritual for one's own ancestors;
then he should give a gentle cow to a Brahmin who is a devotee of Indra.

310 The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, just as when a great rain cloud pours down rain, the water that falls upon the mountain peaks flows down toward the lower valleys; in the same way, Ānanda, those who have not yet attained the fruit of stream-entry, having heard this Dharma-discourse, will all attain the fruit of stream-entry. Those who have not yet attained the fruit of once-returning will attain the fruit of once-returning. Those who have not yet attained the fruit of non-returning will attain the fruit of non-returning. Those who have not yet attained arhatship will attain arhatship. Those who have not yet entered the fixed course of rightness will enter the fixed course of rightness. And those who have already entered the fixed course of rightness will, by means of this Dharma-discourse, advance further along the path. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is wonderful! It is marvelous! How this Dharma-discourse, when taught by the Blessed One, brings such great benefit to sentient beings! The Blessed One said: “So it is, Ānanda. This Dharma-discourse is indeed of great benefit to sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if one were to write down this Dharma-discourse, read it, recite it, and explain its meaning to others, the merit derived from that would be even greater than the former. Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said: “Blessed One, I shall now write down this Dharma-discourse, read it, recite it, and explain its meaning to others. The Blessed One said: “Well done, well done, Ānanda! You should do so. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is the supreme jewel among all dharmas.

It is the unsurpassed medicine for all afflictions. It is the lamp that dispels the darkness of ignorance. It is the bridge for crossing over the great river of saṃsāra. It is the sword that cuts through the net of views. It is the chariot that carries one to the city of Nirvāṇa. Therefore, Ānanda, you should preserve this Dharma-discourse with great care, lest it be lost or forgotten. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. The Venerable Ānanda, having received these instructions from the Blessed One, took up this Dharma-discourse and, throughout his life, diligently practiced it, teaching it to others and ensuring its preservation for the sake of future generations. * 241 * The Blessed One said this: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower growing in a pond; the person who is like a blue lotus flower growing in a pond; the person who is like a white lotus flower growing in a pond; and the person who is like a red lotus flower growing in a pond. And how, Ānanda, is a person like a lotus flower? Here, Ānanda, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Yet, when another person points out to him the danger of sensual lust, he quickly abandons that sensual lust. Just as a blue, red, or white lotus flower born in water and grown in water rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water, even so, Ānanda, is a person like a lotus flower.

This, Ānanda, is called a person like a lotus flower. “And how, Ānanda, is a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, Ānanda, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Yet, when another person points out to him the danger of sensual lust, he does not quickly abandon that sensual lust, but rather reflects upon it repeatedly. Just as a blue lotus flower born in water and grown in water remains submerged at the same level as the water, even so, Ānanda, is a person like a blue lotus flower. This, Ānanda, is called a person like a blue lotus flower. “And how, Ānanda, is a person like a white lotus flower? Here, Ānanda, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Yet, when another person points out to him the danger of sensual lust, he does not quickly abandon that sensual lust, nor does he reflect upon it repeatedly, but rather he endures it for a long time. Just as a white lotus flower born in water and grown in water remains submerged deep within the water, even so, Ānanda, is a person like a white lotus flower. This, Ānanda, is called a person like a white lotus flower. “And how, Ānanda, is a person like a red lotus flower? Here, Ānanda, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Yet, when another person points out to him the danger of sensual lust, he does not quickly abandon that sensual lust, nor does he reflect upon it repeatedly, nor does he endure it for a long time, but rather he indulges in sensual pleasures excessively. Just as a red lotus flower born in water and grown in water remains submerged deep within the water, even so, Ānanda, is a person like a red lotus flower. This, Ānanda, is called a person like a red lotus flower. “These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

104. "The Blessed One has said: 'Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. This was said by the Blessed One. With reference to what was it said? Herein, monks, one person is born into a low family, with little food and drink, with meager sustenance, where food and clothing are obtained with difficulty; that is, among outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or flower-scavengers. He is ugly, unsightly, and deformed, with limbs that are not well-proportioned, with a body that is not well-formed, with a face that is not handsome, with a complexion that is not clear, and he is weak and lacking in strength. Furthermore, he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, seats, or dwellings. This is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, one person is born into a low family... [as above] ...and he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, seats, or dwellings. However, he is wise, intelligent, and possesses discernment; he is capable of understanding the meaning of what is said and of comprehending the Dhamma. This is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, one person is born into a high family, with abundant food and drink, with ample sustenance, where food and clothing are obtained without difficulty; that is, among Khattiyas, Brahmins, or householders. He is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, with limbs that are well-proportioned, with a body that is well-formed, with a face that is handsome, with a complexion that is clear, and he is strong and possessed of great power. Furthermore, he obtains food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, seats, and dwellings. However, he is not wise, not intelligent, and lacks discernment; he is incapable of understanding the meaning of what is said and of comprehending the Dhamma. This is called the third kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, one person is born into a high family... [as above] ...and he obtains food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, seats, and dwellings. Moreover, he is wise, intelligent, and possesses discernment; he is capable of understanding the meaning of what is said and of comprehending the Dhamma. This is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has spoken in brief regarding these four kinds of persons, and having spoken thus, he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling without explaining the detailed meaning. Now, friends, who among us would expand upon the detailed meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One? When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, I shall expand upon the detailed meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One."—"Then let the Venerable Sāriputta speak," they replied. "Listen, friend, and attend closely; I shall speak."—"Yes, friend," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this: "In this case, friend, one person is born into a low family... [as above] ...and he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, seats, or dwellings. He is not wise, not intelligent, and lacks discernment; he is incapable of understanding the meaning of what is said and of comprehending the Dhamma. 31. * The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is because of this that the Tathāgata has declared: ‘Monks, there are these four places that should be visited by a faithful son or daughter of good family with a sense of urgency. What are the four? They are: the place where the Tathāgata was born; the place where the Tathāgata attained supreme and perfect enlightenment; the place where the Tathāgata set in motion the wheel of the Dharma; and the place where the Tathāgata attained final Nirvāṇa through the element of Parinirvāṇa. These, Ānanda, are the four places that should be visited by a faithful son or daughter of good family with a sense of urgency. Then the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: “Lord, may we, having paid homage to the remains of the Tathāgata, go forth to those four places? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, you may go as you wish. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having paid homage to the remains of the Blessed One, departed for those four places. Having arrived at each of them, he paid homage to the remains of the Tathāgata and performed acts of veneration. Having done so, he returned to the presence of the Blessed One. Upon arrival, he prostrated himself at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Lord, I have paid homage to the remains of the Tathāgata at those four places and performed acts of veneration. Lord, what is the destiny of those beings who, having paid homage to the remains of the Tathāgata at those four places, perform acts of veneration?
